title: Era 5 Quizzes (The Nineteenth Century) — Batch 6 of 7
subtitle: Questions 1–250 · Authenticated UGC NET Stems, Keys & Explanations

items.title: Quiz Q#1251 · Walter Pater
items.stem: In which landmark 1873 work of aesthetic criticism does Walter Pater celebrate the sensory, impressionistic appreciation of art through individual essays on Leonardo da Vinci, Botticelli, and Michelangelo?
options: Studies in the History of the Renaissance
items.explanation: Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873) was Walter Pater's seminal manifesto of Aestheticism, urging the critic to cultivate intense sensory and intellectual impressions.

items.title: Quiz Q#1252 · Walter Pater
items.stem: Which Victorian aesthetic critic concluded his 1873 Renaissance studies with the famous manifesto: "To burn always with this hard, gemlike flame, to maintain this ecstasy, is success in life"?
items.explanation: Walter Pater wrote this iconic aesthetic creed in the Conclusion to Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873), asserting that intense fleeting experiences are their own justification.

items.title: Quiz Q#1253 · Walter Pater
items.stem: Which influential 1873 book by Walter Pater had its controversial Conclusion temporarily withdrawn in its second edition (1877) because Pater feared it might mislead young Oxford students into moral hedonism?
options: Studies in the History of the Renaissance
items.explanation: Pater omitted the Conclusion from the 1877 second edition of The Renaissance (re-titling it The Renaissance: Studies in Art and Poetry), restoring it with slight revisions in 1888.

items.title: Quiz Q#1254 · Walter Pater
items.stem: In which 1885 philosophical novel by Walter Pater does a young Roman nobleman in the Antonine era explore Epicurean sensation and Stoicism before being moved by the aesthetic beauty of early Christian worship?
items.explanation: Marius the Epicurean (1885) is Pater's historical novel exploring intellectual and spiritual sensations in second-century Rome, written partly to clarify the serious moral basis of his aestheticism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1255 · Walter Pater
items.stem: Published in two volumes by Macmillan in 1885, which philosophical novel by Walter Pater was written to provide a deeper, more disciplined spiritual exposition of the aesthetic philosophy sketched in The Renaissance?
items.explanation: Marius the Epicurean: His Sensations and Ideas (1885) tracing Marius's spiritual quest under Emperor Marcus Aurelius is Pater's most substantial prose narrative.

items.title: Quiz Q#1256 · Walter Pater
items.stem: In which 1889 volume of literary criticism did Walter Pater publish his celebrated essay 'Style', defining artistic prose as an organic architecture achieved through 'the removal of all surplusage'?
options: Studies in the History of the Renaissance
items.explanation: Appreciations, with an Essay on Style (1889) collects Pater's major literary criticism on Wordsworth, Coleridge, Charles Lamb, Sir Thomas Browne, and Shakespeare.

items.title: Quiz Q#1257 · Walter Pater
items.stem: Which Victorian critic and prose stylist declared in his seminal 1889 essay 'Style' that true literary mastery consists in "the removal of surplusage... leaving the focus of light free for the full expression of meaning"?
items.explanation: Walter Pater opened Appreciations (1889) with his essay 'Style', advocating scrupulous verbal precision, architectural harmony, and the elimination of superfluous ornament.

items.title: Quiz Q#1258 · Walter Pater
items.stem: Containing major critical appreciations of Wordsworth, Coleridge, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti, which 1889 collection by Walter Pater included a controversial essay on 'Aesthetic Poetry' that was suppressed in later editions?
options: Studies in the History of the Renaissance
items.explanation: Appreciations (1889) included Pater's essay 'Aesthetic Poetry' (originally written on William Morris in 1868), which Pater prudently removed from the 1890 second edition.

items.title: Quiz Q#1259 · Arthur Sullivan
items.stem: In which 1875 comic opera with music by Arthur Sullivan and libretto by W. S. Gilbert does Angelina bring a courtroom lawsuit against her fickle fiancé Edwin for breach of promise of marriage?
items.explanation: Trial by Jury (1875) was Arthur Sullivan and W. S. Gilbert's breakout collaboration, composed entirely without spoken dialogue, satirizing legal corruption and Victorian romance.

items.title: Quiz Q#1260 · Arthur Sullivan
items.stem: Premiered at London's Royalty Theatre on 25 March 1875 under Richard D'Oyly Carte's management, which one-act dramatic cantata established the historic creative partnership of Sullivan and Gilbert?
items.explanation: Trial by Jury (1875) was scored by Arthur Sullivan in just a few weeks, becoming a runaway sensation that launched the Savoy Opera tradition.

items.title: Quiz Q#1261 · Arthur Sullivan
items.stem: In which 1878 comic opera scored by Arthur Sullivan does the common sailor Ralph Rackstraw fall in love with his captain's daughter Josephine, defying the aristocratic claims of Sir Joseph Porter?
items.explanation: H.M.S. Pinafore (1878) features Sullivan's brilliant nautical melodies and parody of grand opera conventions, centering on Ralph Rackstraw and Josephine's forbidden love across class barriers.

items.title: Quiz Q#1262 · Arthur Sullivan
items.stem: Which Victorian composer set to music the famous nautical patter song opening: "I am the Captain of the Pinafore; / And a right good captain, too! / And I'm never, never sick at sea! / What, never? / No, never! / What, never? / Well, hardly ever!"?
items.explanation: Sir Arthur Sullivan (1842–1900) composed the sparkling operatic score for H.M.S. Pinafore (1878), creating some of the most enduring comic melodies in English music.

items.title: Quiz Q#1263 · Arthur Sullivan
items.stem: First performed at the Opera Comique on 25 May 1878 and running for 571 performances, which nautical collaboration between Arthur Sullivan and W. S. Gilbert proved to be their first international smash hit?
items.explanation: H.M.S. Pinafore; or, The Lass That Loved a Sailor (1878) was so popular that Sullivan conducted orchestral arrangements of its tunes at the Covent Garden Promenade Concerts.

items.title: Quiz Q#1264 · Arthur Sullivan
items.stem: In which 1885 Savoy Opera by Sullivan and Gilbert does the Mikado's son Nanki-Poo travel disguised as a wandering minstrel to escape marriage with Katisha and wed Yum-Yum in the town of Titipu?
items.explanation: The Mikado (1885) features Sullivan's sophisticated musical parody of faux-Japanese motifs (including the authentic Japanese march 'Miya Sama') paired with Gilbert's satirical libretto.

items.title: Quiz Q#1265 · Arthur Sullivan
items.stem: Premiered at the Savoy Theatre in March 1885, which masterpiece by Arthur Sullivan and W. S. Gilbert remains the most frequently performed Savoy Opera in musical theater history?
items.explanation: The Mikado: or, The Town of Titipu ran for 672 performances at the Savoy Theatre, achieving unprecedented worldwide popularity and critical acclaim for Sullivan's orchestrations.

items.title: Quiz Q#1266 · Henry James
items.stem: In which 1878 novella by Henry James does the fresh, socially innocent young American woman Daisy Miller incur the harsh censure of the Europeanized American expatriate colony in Rome and Geneva?
items.explanation: Daisy Miller (1878) is Henry James's celebrated study of American innocence encountering European social rigidity, narrated through the conflicted perspective of Frederick Winterbourne.

items.title: Quiz Q#1267 · Henry James
items.stem: Which Anglo-American novelist wrote the 1878 international novella in which Winterbourne defines the young American heroine as "a pretty American flirt... an innocent flirt, but still a flirt"?
items.explanation: Henry James explored the misunderstanding of American innocence by sophisticated Europeanized society in Daisy Miller: A Study (1878).

items.title: Quiz Q#1268 · Henry James
items.stem: First serialized in Leslie Stephen's Cornhill Magazine in 1878 before becoming an instant bestseller in England and America, which novella established Henry James's early international fame?
items.explanation: Daisy Miller (1878) gave James his first major popular success, establishing his trademark 'international theme' of the collision between fresh American innocence and European experience.

items.title: Quiz Q#1269 · Henry James
items.stem: In which 1881 masterpiece by Henry James does the independent young American heiress Isabel Archer reject worthy suitors like Lord Warburton, only to be deceived into marriage with the dilettante Gilbert Osmond?
items.explanation: Isabel Archer is the tragic heroine of The Portrait of a Lady (1881). Her idealism and desire for freedom are exploited by Madame Merle and the cold aesthetician Gilbert Osmond.

items.title: Quiz Q#1270 · Henry James
items.stem: Which novelist created the heroine Isabel Archer, who early in her European journey declares to her suitor Caspar Goodwood: "I am very fond of my liberty... I wish to choose my own fate"?
items.explanation: Henry James depicted Isabel Archer's profound commitment to autonomy in The Portrait of a Lady (1881), culminating in her famous nocturnal vigil in Chapter 42.

items.title: Quiz Q#1271 · Henry James
items.stem: Serialized simultaneously in Macmillan's Magazine in London and The Atlantic Monthly in Boston in 1880–1881, which novel is celebrated as the supreme achievement of Henry James's early period?
items.explanation: The Portrait of a Lady (1881) was published in three volumes by Macmillan, celebrated for its intricate psychological realism and Isabel's moral choices.

items.title: Quiz Q#1272 · Henry James
items.stem: In which 1886 novel by Henry James do the fervent Boston feminist Olive Chancellor and the conservative Southern lawyer Basil Ransom contend for the affection and public voice of the gifted orator Verena Tarrant?
items.explanation: The Bostonians (1886) is James's biting satire of post-Civil War American reform movements, depicting the intense psychological rivalry between Olive Chancellor and Basil Ransom over Verena Tarrant.

items.title: Quiz Q#1273 · Henry James
items.stem: Who is the author of the 1886 American novel The Bostonians, depicting the intense ideological and personal struggle over the young feminist speaker Verena Tarrant?
items.explanation: Henry James published The Bostonians in 1886, drawing upon his observations of the New England women's movement and spiritualist circles.

items.title: Quiz Q#1274 · Henry James
items.stem: Serialized in The Century Magazine from February 1885 to February 1886, which Henry James novel was his most panoramic and politically candid exploration of American life and the women's suffrage movement?
items.explanation: The Bostonians (1886) was James's ambitious attempt to write a very American tale exploring the 'decline of the sentiment of sex' and modern political feminism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1275 · Henry James
items.stem: In which 1898 psychological gothic novella by Henry James does an unnamed young governess at the remote Bly country estate become convinced that the children Miles and Flora are being corrupted by the ghosts of Peter Quint and Miss Jessel?
items.explanation: The Turn of the Screw (1898) is James's masterwork of psychological ambiguity, leaving readers to question whether the ghosts are real supernatural entities or hallucinations of the neurotic governess.

items.title: Quiz Q#1276 · Henry James
items.stem: In which masterpiece of psychological horror by Henry James does the governess hold young Miles in her arms during the climactic scene, crying: "Peter Quint, you devil!" as the boy's heart stops?
items.explanation: The tragic final confrontation of The Turn of the Screw (1898) ends with the death of ten-year-old Miles in the governess's desperate grasp.

items.title: Quiz Q#1277 · Henry James
items.stem: Serialized in Collier's Weekly in 1898 with illustrations by John La Farge, which novella by Henry James remains one of the most rigorously debated ghost stories in world literature?
items.explanation: The Turn of the Screw appeared in Collier's Weekly (January–April 1898). Critic Edmund Wilson famously initiated the psychoanalytic reading that the ghosts exist only in the governess's mind.

items.title: Quiz Q#1278 · Edward Carpenter
items.stem: In which epic visionary poem in Whitmanesque free verse did Victorian utopian socialist and philosopher Edward Carpenter advocate sexual emancipation, fellowship with nature, and a non-coercive society?
items.explanation: Towards Democracy (published in stages from 1883 to 1902) was Edward Carpenter's life-work, composed in free verse inspired by Walt Whitman to prophesy an egalitarian democratic socialist society.

items.title: Quiz Q#1279 · Edward Carpenter
items.stem: First published in 1883 by John Heywood and steadily expanded in successive editions through 1902, which magnum opus by Edward Carpenter was described as the poetic bible of the early British socialist and labor movements?
items.explanation: Towards Democracy was deeply influential among early British socialists, Fabians, and labor leaders, advocating simplicity of life, environmentalism, and sexual liberation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1280 · Edward Carpenter
items.stem: In which pioneering 1908 treatise did Edward Carpenter offer a sympathetic, progressive psychological defense of homosexuality, coining the term 'the Intermediate Sex' based on Karl Heinrich Ulrichs's theories?
items.explanation: The Intermediate Sex: A Study of Some Transitional Types of Men and Women (1908) was one of the earliest English books to argue for the social and moral validity of same-sex love.

items.title: Quiz Q#1281 · Edward Carpenter
items.stem: Which Victorian social reformer and philosopher advocated sexual equality and democratic fellowship in The Intermediate Sex (1908), declaring that: "Eros is a great leveller: perhaps the greatest of all levellers"?
items.explanation: Edward Carpenter (1844–1929) was a pioneer of gay rights, vegetarianism, and democratic socialism who lived openly with his working-class partner George Merrill in Derbyshire.

items.title: Quiz Q#1282 · Edward Carpenter
items.stem: Published in London in 1908 by Swan Sonnenschein, which groundbreaking work by Edward Carpenter argued that individuals of intermediate gender temperament often serve as vital social, artistic, and spiritual reconcilers?
items.explanation: The Intermediate Sex (1908) argued that Uranian or homosexual individuals possess unique emotional and intuitive gifts bridging traditional masculine and feminine divisions.

items.title: Quiz Q#1283 · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: In which 1877 sonnet does Jesuit poet Gerard Manley Hopkins celebrate the inexhaustible vitality of the divine presence in nature, despite humanity's industrial smearing and soilure?
items.explanation: 'God's Grandeur' (composed 1877) is Hopkins's celebrated Italian sonnet affirming that 'nature is never spent; / There lives the dearest freshness deep down things' because the Holy Ghost broods over the world.

items.title: Quiz Q#1284 · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: Which Victorian poet composed the incandescent nature sonnet concluding: "Because the Holy Ghost over the bent / World broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings"?
items.explanation: Gerard Manley Hopkins composed these celebrated closing lines in 'God's Grandeur' (1877), using sprung rhythm and alliterative density to celebrate divine immanence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1285 · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: Composed at St. Beuno's College in North Wales in February 1877, which iconic sonnet by Gerard Manley Hopkins opens with the line: "The world is charged with the grandeur of God"?
items.explanation: 'God's Grandeur' was written during Hopkins's theological studies in Wales, showcasing his concepts of 'inscape' (the unique inner design of each created thing) and 'instress'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1286 · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: In which 35-stanza masterpiece of 'sprung rhythm' did Gerard Manley Hopkins commemorate the tragic drowning of five Franciscan nuns exiled from Germany aboard a shipwrecked steamship in the Thames estuary?
items.explanation: The Wreck of the Deutschland (composed winter 1875–1876) broke Hopkins's seven-year poetic silence, transforming the shipwreck into a profound meditation on divine mercy and Christ's suffering.

items.title: Quiz Q#1287 · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: Rejected in 1876 by the Jesuit periodical The Month because its revolutionary metrical experiments were deemed too daring, which great ode by Gerard Manley Hopkins inaugurated his radical use of 'sprung rhythm'?
items.explanation: The Wreck of the Deutschland was rejected by Father Coleridge at The Month. It remained unpublished until Robert Bridges included it in Hopkins's 1918 posthumous Poems.

items.title: Quiz Q#1288 · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: Which Victorian poet opened his famous curtal sonnet 'Pied Beauty' with the hymn: "Glory be to God for dappled things – / For skies of couple-colour as a brinded cow; / For rose-moles all in stipple upon trout that swim..."?
items.explanation: Gerard Manley Hopkins composed 'Pied Beauty' in 1877 using the 'curtal sonnet' form (10.5 lines), praising God for mutability, contrast, and variegated design in creation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1289 · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Gerard Manley Hopkins
items.stem: Edited and published posthumously in 1918 by Poet Laureate Robert Bridges nearly thirty years after the author's death, which landmark volume introduced the revolutionary verse of Gerard Manley Hopkins to the modern world?
items.explanation: Robert Bridges preserved Hopkins's manuscripts and published Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins in 1918. The volume revolutionized 20th-century modernist poetics.

items.title: Quiz Q#1290 · Bram Stoker
items.stem: In which 1897 epistolary gothic novel by Bram Stoker does a Transylvanian undead aristocrat attempt to relocate to London, opposed by Abraham Van Helsing and Jonathan Harker?
options: The Lair of the White Worm
items.explanation: Count Dracula is the title vampire of Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897). The novel is constructed entirely through letters, diary entries, telegrams, and ship's logs.

items.title: Quiz Q#1291 · Bram Stoker
items.stem: Which Victorian author created the sinister Transylvanian nobleman who ominously bids his guest listen to howling wolves: "Listen to them—the children of the night. What music they make!"?
items.explanation: Bram Stoker puts this chilling line into Count Dracula's mouth in Chapter 2 of Dracula (1897) as Jonathan Harker is held captive in Castle Dracula.

items.title: Quiz Q#1292 · Bram Stoker
items.stem: Published in yellow cloth covers by Archibald Constable in London in May 1897, which masterpiece of late-Victorian invasion anxiety and imperial gothic was written by Bram Stoker?
items.explanation: Dracula (1897) drew on European folklore and Emily Gerard's The Land Beyond the Forest, capturing Victorian cultural anxieties concerning reverse colonization and degenerate modernity.

items.title: Quiz Q#1293 · Bram Stoker
items.stem: In which 1903 gothic horror novel by Bram Stoker does the Egyptologist Abel Trelawny attempt the perilous resurrection of the ancient Egyptian Queen Tera in a lonely house in Cornwall?
options: The Lair of the White Worm
items.explanation: The Jewel of Seven Stars (1903) features barrister Malcolm Ross and Margaret Trelawny as they witness the terrifying supernatural powers of the resurrected sorceress Queen Tera.

items.title: Quiz Q#1294 · Bram Stoker
items.stem: Which 1903 archeological horror novel by Bram Stoker had its original bleak ending—in which all the experimenters perish—censored and rewritten with a conventional happy conclusion for its 1912 reissue?
options: The Lair of the White Worm
items.explanation: Heinemann forced Stoker to soften the nihilistic 1903 ending of The Jewel of Seven Stars, where Queen Tera's astral resurrection slaughtered everyone in the chamber.

items.title: Quiz Q#1295 · Romesh Chunder Dutt
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Romesh Chunder Dutt
items.stem: Which pioneering 1877 literary history by Indian civil servant and scholar Romesh Chunder Dutt was the first comprehensive English-language study of Bengali literature from Jayadeva to Michael Madhusudan Dutt?
options: A History of Civilization in Ancient India
items.explanation: The Literature of Bengal (1877) was published under the pseudonym 'Ar Cy D.' (and reissued in 1895 under Dutt's own name), establishing the vernacular literary canon of Bengal for English readers.

items.title: Quiz Q#1296 · Romesh Chunder Dutt
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Romesh Chunder Dutt
items.stem: Published in London by T. Fisher Unwin in 1902, which domestic novel by Romesh Chunder Dutt (translated by the author from his Bengali novel Sansar) depicted rural Bengali domestic life and Hindu widow remarriage?
items.explanation: The Lake of Palms: A Story of Indian Domestic Life (1902) was Romesh Chunder Dutt's English translation of his Bengali reformist novel Sansar (1886), addressing the tragic plight of young Hindu widows.

items.title: Quiz Q#1297 · Kate Chopin
items.stem: In which 1894 regionalist short story collection by Kate Chopin does the tragic tale 'Désirée's Baby' depict a young mother driven to suicide with her child when her husband wrongly accuses her of mixed racial heritage?
items.explanation: Bayou Folk (1894) is Kate Chopin's celebrated collection of twenty-three Louisiana Creole and Cajun local color stories, featuring 'Désirée's Baby' and 'Madame Célestin's Divorce'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1298 · Kate Chopin
items.stem: Which 19th-century American author wrote the devastating southern local-color story 'Désirée's Baby', in which Armand Aubigny discovers too late that it was his own mother who was of African descent?
items.explanation: Kate Chopin included 'Désirée's Baby' in Bayou Folk (1894). The story concludes with Armand reading a letter from his deceased mother thanking God that Armand will never know she belonged to the enslaved race.

items.title: Quiz Q#1299 · Kate Chopin
items.stem: Published in Boston by Houghton, Mifflin in 1894, which debut story collection established Kate Chopin's national reputation as a master of Louisiana Creole and Acadian dialect and culture?
items.explanation: Bayou Folk (1894) was praised by contemporary critics for its authentic depiction of Natchitoches Parish life and its sophisticated psychological realism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1300 · Kate Chopin
items.stem: In which landmark 1899 novella by Kate Chopin does the heroine Edna Pontellier experience an intellectual, artistic, and sensual awakening on Grand Isle, ultimately choosing to swim out to her death in the Gulf of Mexico?
items.explanation: The Awakening (1899) traces Edna Pontellier's rebellion against conventional marriage and motherhood through her love for Robert Lebrun and her final fatal swim into the sea.

items.title: Quiz Q#1301 · Kate Chopin
items.stem: Which American feminist author opened and closed her controversial 1899 masterpiece with the lyrical motif: "The voice of the sea is seductive; never ceasing, whispering, clamoring, murmuring, inviting the soul to wander for a spell in abysses of solitude"?
items.explanation: Kate Chopin's The Awakening (1899) employs the sea as a recurring symbol of sensual awakening, boundless freedom, and ultimate oblivion.

items.title: Quiz Q#1302 · Kate Chopin
items.stem: Condemned by contemporary Victorian critics as morbid and vulgar for depicting female sexual autonomy, which 1899 masterpiece by Kate Chopin was rediscovered in the 1960s as a foundational American feminist text?
items.explanation: The Awakening was published by Herbert S. Stone in Chicago in April 1899. The hostility of reviewers broke Chopin's literary career, but the novel was restored to classic status by modern feminist scholars.

items.title: Quiz Q#1303 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: In which classic 1883 adventure novel by Robert Louis Stevenson does the young narrator Jim Hawkins discover Billy Bones's treasure map at the Admiral Benbow inn and sail aboard the Hispaniola?
items.explanation: Treasure Island (1883) features Jim Hawkins, the one-legged pirate Long John Silver, Squire Trelawney, and the voyage to recover Captain Flint's buried gold.

items.title: Quiz Q#1304 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: Which Victorian Scottish author immortalized the fictional pirate sea-shanty: "Fifteen men on the dead man's chest— / Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! / Drink and the devil had done for the rest— / Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!"?
items.explanation: Robert Louis Stevenson invented the famous pirate shanty 'Dead Man's Chest' for his 1883 adventure classic Treasure Island.

items.title: Quiz Q#1305 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: First serialized under the pseudonym 'Captain George North' in the boys' magazine Young Folks between 1881 and 1882, which book established Robert Louis Stevenson's international reputation?
items.explanation: Treasure Island appeared as 'The Sea Cook, or Treasure Island' in Young Folks before Cassell published it in book form in 1883, transforming the pirate genre forever.

items.title: Quiz Q#1306 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: In which 1886 historical novel by Robert Louis Stevenson does the orphaned Lowland youth David Balfour get kidnapped by his wicked uncle Ebenezer and flee across the Scottish Highlands with the Jacobite outlaw Alan Breck Stewart?
items.explanation: Kidnapped (1886) recounts David Balfour's survival aboard the Covenant and his flight through the heather with the proud Highlander Alan Breck after the Appin Murder.

items.title: Quiz Q#1307 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: Set in 1751 in the aftermath of the Jacobite Rising of 1745 and featuring the real-life historical mystery of the Appin Murder, which 1886 novel was written by Robert Louis Stevenson?
items.explanation: Kidnapped (1886) was serialized in Young Folks and published by Cassell. Stevenson used the historic shooting of Colin Roy Campbell ('the Red Fox') as the pivot for David and Alan's adventures.

items.title: Quiz Q#1308 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: In which 1886 novella by Robert Louis Stevenson does a respected London physician invent a chemical potion to separate his civilized persona from his depraved, violent alter ego?
options: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
items.explanation: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886) investigates the duality of Victorian man through the lawyer Gabriel John Utterson's pursuit of the monstrous Edward Hyde.

items.title: Quiz Q#1309 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: Originated from a feverish nightmare that the author drafted in three days and then threw into the fire to rewrite entirely, which 1886 allegory by Robert Louis Stevenson sold over 40,000 copies in six months?
options: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
items.explanation: Stevenson's wife Fanny criticized his first draft of Jekyll and Hyde as a mere thriller; he burnt it and rewrote it as the profound psychological allegory of Victorian hypocrisy that was published in January 1886.

items.title: Quiz Q#1310 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: In which dark 1889 historical novel by Robert Louis Stevenson are two Scottish brothers of the Durrisdeer family—the charming, villainous James Durie and the honest, plodding Henry—driven into lethal hatred spanning Scotland, India, and America?
items.explanation: The Master of Ballantrae (1889) traces the fraternal fratricide between James and Henry Durie, narrated by the loyal estate steward Ephraim Mackellar.

items.title: Quiz Q#1311 · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Robert Louis Stevenson
items.stem: Serialized in Scribner's Magazine between 1888 and 1889, which psychological novel set during the Jacobite rebellion concludes with the fatal duel and double death of two brothers in the frozen Adirondack wilderness?
items.explanation: The Master of Ballantrae (1889) was begun in the Adirondack Mountains while Stevenson was undergoing treatment for tuberculosis, culminating in the horrific scene of James's failed exhumation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1312 · Henry Arthur Jones
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Henry Arthur Jones
items.stem: In which sensational 1882 Victorian stage melodrama by Henry Arthur Jones and Henry Herman does the ruined gambler Wilfred Denver flee to America believing he has murdered Geoffrey Ware, later returning as a wealthy philanthropist?
items.explanation: The Silver King (1882) was one of the most successful Victorian melodramas, featuring Wilfred Denver's despair and his celebrated line: 'O God! put back Thy universe and give me yesterday!'

items.title: Quiz Q#1313 · Henry Arthur Jones
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Henry Arthur Jones
items.stem: Which Victorian dramatist created the famous melodrama The Silver King, where the guilt-stricken hero Wilfred Denver cries out in anguish: "O God! put back Thy universe and give me yesterday!"?
items.explanation: Henry Arthur Jones (1851–1929) achieved immense fame and wealth with The Silver King (1882), which Matthew Arnold praised for raising English melodrama toward genuine dramatic literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1314 · Henry Arthur Jones
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Henry Arthur Jones
items.stem: Premiered at the Princess's Theatre on 16 November 1882 starring Wilson Barrett, which play ran for 289 performances and was celebrated by Matthew Arnold as an important step toward modern English dramatic realism?
items.explanation: The Silver King (1882) demonstrated that commercial Victorian theater could combine exciting melodramatic spectacle with psychological pathos and poetic dialogue.

items.title: Quiz Q#1315 · Henry Arthur Jones
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Henry Arthur Jones
items.stem: In which 1897 high-society comedy of manners by Henry Arthur Jones does Sir Christopher Deering intervene to prevent Lady Jessica Nepean from eloping with the romantic explorer Edward Falkner, saving her marriage through comedic deceit?
items.explanation: The Liars (1897) features Sir Christopher Deering managing a chaotic web of society lies concocted by Lady Jessica's friends to conceal her flirtatious dinner at Shepperford.

items.title: Quiz Q#1316 · Henry Arthur Jones
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Henry Arthur Jones
items.stem: Which Victorian dramatist satirized aristocratic deceit in his 1897 society comedy The Liars, where Sir Christopher Deering lectures husbands on domestic harmony: "Flirt with your wife yourself... It's amusing and it saves a world of trouble"?
items.explanation: Henry Arthur Jones was a leading playwright of the Victorian society comedy alongside Arthur Wing Pinero, perfecting witty dialogue in The Liars (1897).

items.title: Quiz Q#1317 · Henry Arthur Jones
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Henry Arthur Jones
items.stem: Premiered at the Criterion Theatre in October 1897 with Charles Wyndham in the lead, which society comedy is regarded by dramatic historians as Henry Arthur Jones's finest achievement in the comedy of manners?
items.explanation: The Liars (1897) ran for nearly 300 performances at the Criterion Theatre, celebrated as a sparkling masterpiece of late-Victorian drawing-room comedy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1318 · Mona Caird
items.stem: In which 1894 New Woman novel by Mona Caird does the aspiring musician Hadria Fullerton find her creative ambitions as a composer stifled by the domestic demands of Victorian marriage and motherhood?
items.explanation: The Daughters of Danaus (1894) is Mona Caird's major feminist novel. Hadria Fullerton's artistic genius is systematically drained by traditional Victorian family expectations.

items.title: Quiz Q#1319 · Mona Caird
items.stem: Published in 1894 by Bliss, Sands, and Foster, which novel by Mona Caird used the Greek myth of the Danaïdes (condemned endlessly to fill leaky sieves with water) as a metaphor for women's futile domestic labor?
options: The Story of an African Farm
items.explanation: The Daughters of Danaus (1894) is a landmark of fin-de-siècle New Woman fiction, critiquing marriage as an institution that sacrifices women's intellectual and creative individuality.

items.title: Quiz Q#1320 · Mona Caird
items.stem: In which 1897 collection of feminist essays did Mona Caird collect her famous polemic 'Marriage' (originally published in the Westminster Review in 1888), which famously described traditional Victorian marriage as a 'vexatious failure'?
items.explanation: The Morality of Marriage and Other Essays on the Status and Destiny of Woman (1897) collected Caird's revolutionary articles attacking economic dependence in marriage and advocating equal partnership.

items.title: Quiz Q#1321 · Mona Caird
items.stem: Whose 1888 Westminster Review article 'Marriage' provoked the Daily Telegraph's famous public debate titled 'Is Marriage a Failure?', receiving over 27,000 letters from Victorian readers?
items.explanation: Mona Caird's radical 1888 essay ignited one of the largest media debates of the late Victorian era, making her one of the foremost feminist polemicists of the 1890s.

items.title: Quiz Q#1322 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Which 1881 debut volume of verse by Oscar Wilde, published in parchment covers with gold blossom designs, contained aesthetic lyrics like 'Impression du Matin' and 'The Harlot's House'?
items.explanation: Poems (1881) was Oscar Wilde's first published book, printed at his own expense by David Bogue, establishing his persona as the flamboyant apostle of the Aesthetic Movement.

items.title: Quiz Q#1323 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Published in London in 1881 when the author was twenty-six, which debut volume led to Oscar Wilde's famous 1882 lecture tour across the United States promoting the English Renaissance of Art?
items.explanation: The publication of Poems (1881) coincided with Gilbert and Sullivan's aesthetic opera Patience, leading Richard D'Oyly Carte to hire Wilde to tour America as the real-life aesthetic dandy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1324 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which 1888 fairy tale collection by Oscar Wilde does the golden, jeweled statue of a deceased prince enlist a compassionate swallow to strip off his gold leaves and ruby sword-hilt to relieve the city's poor?
options: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
items.explanation: The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888) includes 'The Happy Prince', 'The Nightingale and the Rose', 'The Selfish Giant', 'The Devoted Friend', and 'The Remarkable Rocket'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1325 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Which fairy tale by Oscar Wilde features the dying bird who gives its lifeblood to press a red rose from a white thorn for a student, while the narrator reflects on the sacrifice of love?
options: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
items.explanation: 'The Nightingale and the Rose' appears in Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888), blending Hans Christian Andersen's fairy-tale simplicity with decadent aesthetic pathos.

items.title: Quiz Q#1326 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Illustrated by Walter Crane and Jacomb Hood, which 1888 volume was Oscar Wilde's first published work of prose fiction?
options: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
items.explanation: The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888) was praised by contemporary critics including Walter Pater, who admired Wilde's delicate prose rhythms and moral allegories.

items.title: Quiz Q#1327 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which 1890/1891 decadent novel by Oscar Wilde does a narcissistic young aristocrat remain eternally young and unmarked by crime, while his hidden portrait painted by Basil Hallward ages and records his moral corruption?
items.explanation: The Picture of Dorian Gray features Dorian Gray, the cynical dandy Lord Henry Wotton, and the artist Basil Hallward, exploring the deadly consequences of aesthetic hedonism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1328 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Which famous aphorism concludes Oscar Wilde's iconic 1891 Preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray: "We can forgive a man for making a useful thing as long as he does not admire it. The only excuse for making a useless thing is that one admires it intensely. All art is..."?
items.explanation: Wilde added the famous Preface of twenty-three aphorisms to the 1891 book edition of The Picture of Dorian Gray, concluding with the supreme aesthetic doctrine: 'All art is quite useless.'

items.title: Quiz Q#1329 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: First printed in the July 1890 issue of Lippincott's Monthly Magazine before being expanded to twenty chapters with an aesthetic Preface in 1891, which was Oscar Wilde's only novel?
items.explanation: The Picture of Dorian Gray was censored by Lippincott's editor J. M. Stoddart in 1890. Wilde added six chapters, smoothed overtly homoerotic phrases, and added his Preface for Ward, Lock & Co. in April 1891.

items.title: Quiz Q#1330 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which 1892 society comedy by Oscar Wilde does Mrs. Erlynne sacrifice her own reputation to save her daughter Lady Windermere from leaving her husband, revealing maternal love beneath her mercenary exterior?
items.explanation: Lady Windermere's Fan: A Play About a Good Woman (1892) centers on Lady Windermere's puritanical moralism, which is softened by the secret self-sacrifice of her scandalous mother, Mrs. Erlynne.

items.title: Quiz Q#1331 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Which witty character in Oscar Wilde's 1892 comedy Lady Windermere's Fan utters the celebrated epigram: "We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars"?
items.explanation: Lord Darlington speaks this famous aphorism in Act III of Oscar Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan (1892) during a conversation with Cecil Graham and Lord Windermere at his bachelor rooms.

items.title: Quiz Q#1332 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Play About a Good Woman', which 1892 comedy produced at the St. James's Theatre by George Alexander inaugurated Oscar Wilde's brilliant series of late-Victorian society plays?
items.explanation: Lady Windermere's Fan opened on 20 February 1892 at the St. James's Theatre. Wilde famously addressed the opening-night audience with a cigarette in hand, congratulating them on their good taste.

items.title: Quiz Q#1333 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which 1893 society drama by Oscar Wilde does the puritanical Mrs. Rachel Arbuthnot refuse to marry Lord Illingworth, the cynical aristocrat who fathered her illegitimate son Gerald twenty years earlier?
items.explanation: A Woman of No Importance (1893) pits Lord Illingworth's brilliant, amoral aristocratic dandyism against Mrs. Arbuthnot's fierce maternal integrity.

items.title: Quiz Q#1334 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which Oscar Wilde comedy does the cynical dandy Lord Illingworth deliver the famous epigram on family resemblance: "All women become like their mothers. That is their tragedy. No man does. That's his"?
items.explanation: Lord Illingworth delivers this famous cynical witticism in Act III of A Woman of No Importance (1893). Wilde later reused a variation of it in The Importance of Being Earnest.

items.title: Quiz Q#1335 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Premiered at the Haymarket Theatre in April 1893 starring Herbert Beerbohm Tree, which Oscar Wilde play exposed the double standard of Victorian sexual morality through the figure of the 'fallen woman'?
items.explanation: A Woman of No Importance (1893) challenged Victorian hypocrisy by showing Mrs. Arbuthnot striking Lord Illingworth across the face with his own glove and dismissing him as a 'man of no importance'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1336 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which 1893 symbolist tragedy by Oscar Wilde—originally composed in French—does the Judean princess dance the Dance of the Seven Veils before Herod Antipas to demand the severed head of Jokanaan on a silver charger?
items.explanation: Salomé (1893) was written by Wilde in French for Sarah Bernhardt. It is a masterpiece of Decadent symbolism exploring necrophilic passion, prohibited biblical lust, and moon imagery.

items.title: Quiz Q#1337 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Which decadent play by Oscar Wilde reaches its shocking climax when the title heroine passionately kisses the cold lips of the severed head of Jokanaan, crying: "Ah! I have kissed thy mouth, Jokanaan, I have kissed thy mouth"?
items.explanation: This climax of Salomé (1893) horrified Victorian authorities. Herod, terrified by her perversion, orders his soldiers: 'Kill that woman!', crushing her under their shields.

items.title: Quiz Q#1338 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Banned from performance in London in 1892 by the Lord Chamberlain under an ancient law forbidding the stage depiction of biblical characters, which Oscar Wilde play was illustrated by Aubrey Beardsley in 1894?
items.explanation: Salomé was banned in Britain while Sarah Bernhardt was rehearsing it. Lord Alfred Douglas translated it into English, and John Lane published it in 1894 with Beardsley's grotesque art nouveau illustrations.

items.title: Quiz Q#1339 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which 1895 political drama by Oscar Wilde is the virtuous Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, Sir Robert Chiltern, blackmailed by Mrs. Cheveley over a cabinet secret he sold in his youth to fund his political career?
items.explanation: An Ideal Husband (1895) centers on Sir Robert Chiltern's past corruption regarding the Suez Canal. His career and marriage to the puritanical Lady Chiltern are saved by the witty dandy Lord Goring.

items.title: Quiz Q#1340 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Which character in Oscar Wilde's An Ideal Husband serves as the author's philosophical mouthpiece, defined as a dandy who "plays with life" and famously remarks: "To love oneself is the beginning of a lifelong romance"?
items.explanation: Lord Goring is Wilde's supreme dramatic embodiment of the philosophical dandy, combining superficial indolence with profound emotional intelligence and practical loyalty.

items.title: Quiz Q#1341 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Opening at the Haymarket Theatre on 3 January 1895, which play by Oscar Wilde addressed political blackmail, insider trading, and the impossibility of measuring human love against impossible standards of perfection?
items.explanation: An Ideal Husband (1895) was praised by George Bernard Shaw for its sharp political wit, exposing how English public life was compromised by secret financial corruption.

items.title: Quiz Q#1342 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: In which 1895 farce by Oscar Wilde do Jack Worthing and Algernon Moncrieff practice 'Bunburying' to escape tedious social duties, leading to farcical complications over the name 'Ernest'?
items.explanation: The Importance of Being Earnest (1895) is Wilde's masterpiece of high farce, featuring Jack Worthing, Algernon Moncrieff, Gwendolen Fairfax, Cecily Cardew, and Lady Bracknell.

items.title: Quiz Q#1343 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Which iconic character in The Importance of Being Earnest utters the famous epigram: "The truth is rarely pure and never simple. Modern life would be very tedious if it were either..."?
items.explanation: Algernon Moncrieff makes this famous assertion to Jack Worthing in Act I of Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest (1895) when interrogating Jack about his engraved cigarette case.

items.title: Quiz Q#1344 · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Trivial Comedy for Serious People', which 1895 theatrical masterpiece by Oscar Wilde features the famous interrogation of Jack Worthing by Lady Bracknell regarding his birth in a handbag at Victoria Station?
items.explanation: The Importance of Being Earnest premiered on 14 February 1895 at the St. James's Theatre. Lady Bracknell's line—'To lose one parent, Mr. Worthing, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness'—is one of the most famous in English comedy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1345 · Sarah Grand
items.stem: In which 1893 New Woman novel by Sarah Grand does the educated heroine Evadne Frayling discover on her wedding day that her husband Major Colquhoun has led a dissolute life, refusing to consummate the marriage?
items.explanation: The Heavenly Twins (1893) is Sarah Grand's landmark feminist novel exploring the tragic consequences of the Victorian sexual double standard and syphilitic infection through Evadne, Edith, and Angelica.

items.title: Quiz Q#1346 · Sarah Grand
items.stem: Which New Woman novelist popularized the term 'New Woman' in an 1894 North American Review article ('The New Aspect of the Woman Question') following the runaway success of her 1893 novel The Heavenly Twins?
items.explanation: Sarah Grand (Frances Elizabeth Bellenden Clarke, 1854–1943) coined the phrase 'The New Woman' in response to Ouida, defending modern women who demanded moral purity and intellectual autonomy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1347 · Sarah Grand
items.stem: Published in three volumes by William Heinemann in 1893, which bestselling novel sold over 20,000 copies in a few months, becoming the definitive fictional manifesto of the New Woman movement?
items.explanation: The Heavenly Twins (1893) created an enormous cultural stir with its unvarnished exposure of venereal disease brought into innocent marriages by corrupt aristocratic men.

items.title: Quiz Q#1348 · Sarah Grand
items.stem: In which 1897 autobiographical New Woman novel by Sarah Grand does the creative heroine Elizabeth Caldwell Maclure ('Beth') break free from an abusive husband who runs a lock hospital to become a celebrated feminist orator?
items.explanation: The Beth Book: Being a Study from the Life of Elizabeth Caldwell Maclure (1897) is Grand's semi-autobiographical bildungsroman, chronicling Beth's artistic development and rebellion against patriarchal medical power.

items.title: Quiz Q#1349 · Sarah Grand
items.stem: Subtitled 'Being a Study from the Life of Elizabeth Caldwell Maclure', which 1897 novel by Sarah Grand provides an unsparing feminist critique of Victorian child-rearing and the Contagious Diseases Acts?
items.explanation: The Beth Book was published by Heinemann in 1897, attacking the institutionalized sexual exploitation of women and documenting Beth's realization of her literary vocation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1350 · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.stem: In which 1893 drama by Arthur Wing Pinero does the respectable widower Aubrey Tanqueray marry Paula, a 'woman with a past', only for high society to ostracize them until Paula is driven to suicide?
items.explanation: The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893) made theatrical history. Paula Tanqueray's despair over social exclusion and the sudden return of her former lover Captain Ardale leads to her suicide.

items.title: Quiz Q#1351 · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.stem: Which Victorian dramatist created the tragic heroine Paula Tanqueray, who utters the fatalistic realization: "The future is only the past again, entered through another gate"?
items.explanation: Sir Arthur Wing Pinero (1855–1934) wrote this famous line in Act IV of The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893), illustrating the impossibility for a Victorian woman of outliving her sexual past.

items.title: Quiz Q#1352 · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.stem: Premiered at London's St. James's Theatre in May 1893 and making an overnight star of Mrs. Patrick Campbell in the title role, which play is widely recognized as inaugurating modern English problem drama?
items.explanation: The Second Mrs Tanqueray (1893) revolutionized the Victorian stage, introducing Ibsenite psychological realism and social problem drama into the commercial West End.

items.title: Quiz Q#1353 · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.stem: In which 1898 affectionate backstage comedy by Arthur Wing Pinero does the young actress Rose Trelawny leave the boisterous melodrama troupe at the Bagnigge Wells theatre to marry into an austere aristocratic family in Cavendish Square?
items.explanation: Trelawny of the 'Wells' (1898) is Pinero's nostalgic tribute to the 1860s theatrical revolution led by playwright Tom Robertson (fictionalized as Tom Wrench), who pioneered realistic 'cup-and-saucer' drama.

items.title: Quiz Q#1354 · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.stem: Which Victorian playwright commemorated the realistic theatrical reforms of Tom Robertson in his celebrated 1898 backstage comedy Trelawny of the 'Wells'?
items.explanation: Arthur Wing Pinero drew upon his own early years as an actor to write Trelawny of the 'Wells' (1898), contrasting the old, artificial declamatory stagecraft with modern naturalistic acting.

items.title: Quiz Q#1355 · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Wing Pinero
items.stem: First performed at the Royal Court Theatre in January 1898, which beloved theatrical comedy by Arthur Wing Pinero dramatizes the historical transition from Victorian theatrical bombast to intimate drawing-room realism?
items.explanation: Trelawny of the 'Wells' remains one of Pinero's most frequently revived works, celebrating the magic of theatrical life and the birth of realistic modern staging.

items.title: Quiz Q#1356 · Marie Corelli
items.stem: In which 1886 occult bestseller by Marie Corelli does an exhausted young female pianist travel to Paris, where the mystic Heliobas introduces her to the 'Electric Principle of Christianity' and astral projection?
items.explanation: A Romance of Two Worlds (1886) was Marie Corelli's sensational debut novel, combining Christian mysticism, electricity, spiritual healing, and Victorian occultism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1357 · Marie Corelli
items.stem: Which bestselling Victorian sensationalist author made her spectacular debut in 1886 with A Romance of Two Worlds, claiming in her preface that electric spiritual forces offer empirical proof of the afterlife?
items.explanation: Marie Corelli (Mary Mackay, 1855–1924) became the bestselling British novelist of the late Victorian era, read by Queen Victoria, Gladstone, and millions of ordinary readers.

items.title: Quiz Q#1358 · Marie Corelli
items.stem: In which 1895 bestselling Faustian novel by Marie Corelli does the starving novelist Geoffrey Tempest inherit five million pounds and fall under the influence of the charismatic, melancholic Prince Lucio Rimânez (Satan in disguise)?
items.explanation: The Sorrows of Satan (1895) features Prince Lucio Rimânez (Lucifer), who is cursed to tempt humanity but grieves each time a human soul falls into his trap.

items.title: Quiz Q#1359 · Marie Corelli
items.stem: Breaking all previous publishing records in English fiction with over 50,000 copies sold in its first seven weeks, which 1895 novel by Marie Corelli attacked corrupt critics, literary cliques, and decadent society?
items.explanation: The Sorrows of Satan; or, The Strange Experience of One Geoffrey Tempest, Millionaire (1895) refused advance review copies to critics, yet became an unprecedented publishing phenomenon.

items.title: Quiz Q#1360 · Olive Schreiner
items.stem: In which 1883 South African colonial novel by Olive Schreiner does the rebellious and intellectually gifted heroine Lyndall reject conventional marriage, declare her spiritual independence, and tragically die in childbirth?
options: The Story of an African Farm
items.explanation: Lyndall is the pioneering feminist heroine of The Story of an African Farm (1883), whose existential dialogue with the gentle Waldo forms the moral core of the novel.

items.title: Quiz Q#1361 · Olive Schreiner
items.stem: Published in London in 1883 under the male pseudonym 'Ralph Iron', which groundbreaking novel set on an isolated Karoo ostrich farm is celebrated as the foundational text of South African literature in English?
options: The Story of an African Farm
items.explanation: The Story of an African Farm (1883) was written by Olive Schreiner while working as an isolated governess on the veld, achieving immediate international acclaim for its feminist and religious unorthodoxy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1362 · Olive Schreiner
items.stem: In which 1890 allegorical collection by Olive Schreiner does the famous parable 'The Hunter' depict a solitary seeker who leaves comfortable traditions behind to climb the snowy mountain peaks in search of the white bird of Truth?
options: The Story of an African Farm
items.explanation: Dreams (1890) collects Schreiner's visionary feminist and philosophical allegories, including 'The Hunter' (first embedded in The Story of an African Farm) and 'Three Dreams in a Desert'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1363 · Olive Schreiner
items.stem: Dedicated to her friend, sexologist Havelock Ellis, which 1890 volume of allegorical prose poems by Olive Schreiner formulated visionary metaphors for the spiritual and economic liberation of women?
options: The Story of an African Farm
items.explanation: Dreams (1890) was acclaimed by contemporary readers, including British suffragettes and Olive Schreiner's lifelong intellectual companion Havelock Ellis, for its poetic power.

items.title: Quiz Q#1364 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In which 1892 debut play by George Bernard Shaw does the idealistic young doctor Harry Trench discover to his horror that his own modest mortgage interest is derived from the miserable rack-rents of London slum tenements?
items.explanation: Widowers' Houses (1892) was the first of Shaw's 'Plays Unpleasant', exposing Sartorius's slum-landlord exploitation and showing how all middle-class income is entangled in social injustice.

items.title: Quiz Q#1365 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Premiered at J. T. Grein's Independent Theatre Society in December 1892, which play was George Bernard Shaw's first produced drama, inaugurating his theatrical career as an Ibsenite social dramatist?
items.explanation: Widowers' Houses (1892) began as a collaboration with dramatic critic William Archer before Shaw completed it alone to inaugurate realistic socialist problem plays in London.

items.title: Quiz Q#1366 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In which 1898 Shavian comedy does Candida Morell choose between her complacent Christian Socialist clergyman husband James and the passionate, frail eighteen-year-old poet Eugene Marchbanks?
items.explanation: Candida (1898), one of Shaw's 'Plays Pleasant', subverts the conventional Victorian love triangle when Candida chooses to remain with her husband because he is secretly the weaker man who needs her more.

items.title: Quiz Q#1367 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Mystery', which 1898 play by George Bernard Shaw parodies domestic melodrama by presenting a sensible, maternal heroine who governs two self-absorbed men?
items.explanation: Candida: A Mystery was written in 1894 and published in Plays Pleasant (1898). Its subtle psychological comedy centers on Candida's maternal mastery over both Morell and Marchbanks.

items.title: Quiz Q#1368 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In which 1903 philosophical drama by George Bernard Shaw does the confirmed bachelor and revolutionary theorist John Tanner find himself relentlessly pursued by Ann Whitefield, who embodies the primal 'Life Force'?
items.explanation: Man and Superman (1903) presents Shaw's creative evolutionary philosophy: woman as the agent of the Life Force pursuing the intellectual man (Don Juan/Tanner) to advance the human species.

items.title: Quiz Q#1369 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Containing the famous third-act dream sequence 'Don Juan in Hell' and the appended philosophical essay 'The Revolutionist's Handbook', which 1903 drama was George Bernard Shaw's philosophical masterpiece?
items.explanation: Man and Superman: A Comedy and a Philosophy (1903) contains 'Don Juan in Hell', a four-way philosophical debate in the underworld between Don Juan, the Devil, Doña Ana, and the Statue.

items.title: Quiz Q#1370 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In which 1913/1916 comedy by George Bernard Shaw does the arrogant phonetician Professor Henry Higgins wager that he can transform the Cockney flower girl Eliza Doolittle into a duchess at an ambassador's garden party?
items.explanation: Pygmalion (1916) is Shaw's famous comedy of social phonetics and class mobility, subverting the Ovidian myth when Eliza achieves complete spiritual independence from her creator Higgins.

items.title: Quiz Q#1371 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: First performed in a German translation at the Burgtheater in Vienna in 1913 before opening in London in 1914 starring Mrs. Patrick Campbell, which Shavian comedy famously caused a sensation with Eliza's exclamation: 'Not bloody likely!'?
items.explanation: Pygmalion caused an enormous theatrical sensation at Her Majesty's Theatre in 1914 when Mrs. Patrick Campbell uttered the forbidden word 'bloody' on the respectable Victorian stage.

items.title: Quiz Q#1372 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: In which 1923 historical chronicle play by George Bernard Shaw is a 15th-century French peasant girl martyred by church inquisitors for her nationalist fervor and direct spiritual communion with God?
items.explanation: Saint Joan (1923) portrays Joan of Arc not as a romantic saint but as an early Protestant martyr, nationalist visionary, and military genius whose trial dramatizes the clash between individual conscience and institutional authority.

items.title: Quiz Q#1373 · George Bernard Shaw
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem: Premiered in New York by the Theatre Guild in December 1923 and concluding with Joan's anguished epilogue plea: "O God that madest this beautiful earth, when will it be ready to receive Thy saints? How long, O Lord, how long?", which play directly earned Shaw the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature?
items.explanation: Saint Joan (1923) was hailed worldwide as Shaw's supreme tragic masterpiece, leading directly to his award of the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#1374 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: In which 1885 imperial adventure romance by H. Rider Haggard do the veteran hunter Allan Quatermain, Sir Henry Curtis, and Captain Good journey into the unexplored African interior to locate a lost brother and biblical diamond mines?
items.explanation: King Solomon's Mines (1885) established the 'lost world' literary genre, following Quatermain's expedition across the desert and mountains into the hidden kingdom of Kukuanaland.

items.title: Quiz Q#1375 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: Which Victorian author opened his 1885 African adventure novel King Solomon's Mines with Allan Quatermain's proud boast that "there is not a petticoat in the whole history", setting a standard for boyish imperial romance?
items.explanation: H. Rider Haggard (1856–1925) wrote King Solomon's Mines on a bet that he could write a story better than Stevenson's Treasure Island, producing a foundational classic of imperial romance.

items.title: Quiz Q#1376 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: Published by Cassell in 1885, which adventure novel by H. Rider Haggard was an immediate publishing sensation, introducing the great African warrior Ignosi and the terrifying ancient witch Gagool?
items.explanation: King Solomon's Mines (1885) sold over 30,000 copies in its first year, establishing Haggard alongside Stevenson as a revitalizer of romantic storytelling against mundane realism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1377 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: In which 1886 fantasy romance by H. Rider Haggard do Horace Holly and his handsome ward Leo Vincey discover the subterranean city of Kôr in East Africa, ruled by the immortal, veil-shrouded sorceress Ayesha?
items.explanation: She: A History of Adventure (1886) depicts Ayesha, the two-thousand-year-old queen who has bathed in the Pillar of Life and waits for the reincarnation of her lost lover Kallikrates.

items.title: Quiz Q#1378 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: Which Victorian author created the immortal, terrifying sorceress-queen Ayesha, known throughout the lost subterranean empire of Kôr as "She-who-must-be-obeyed"?
items.explanation: H. Rider Haggard created Ayesha ('She-who-must-be-obeyed') in She (1886). The novel profoundly influenced psychoanalytic theorists Sigmund Freud and C. G. Jung as an archetype of the anima.

items.title: Quiz Q#1379 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: Serialized in The Graphic in 1886 before becoming an international bestseller, which gothic romance by H. Rider Haggard dramatizes the tragic dissolution of Queen Ayesha in the Pillar of Life?
items.explanation: She (1886) was one of the bestselling novels in Victorian history, praised by Andrew Lang and Henry James for its hypnotic imaginative myth-making.

items.title: Quiz Q#1380 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: In which 1887 sequel by H. Rider Haggard does the aging elephant-hunter Allan Quatermain, mourning the death of his only son, lead one last expedition to find the lost white race of Zu-Vendis?
items.explanation: Allan Quatermain (1887) recounts Quatermain's final journey with Sir Henry Curtis and Umslopogaas to the subterranean kingdom of Zu-Vendis, ending with Quatermain's death.

items.title: Quiz Q#1381 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: Which Victorian adventure writer concluded his 1887 novel Allan Quatermain with the dying hero's noble words of resignation: "Who am I that I should complain? I have lived a long and full life... and now I am going home"?
items.explanation: H. Rider Haggard dedicated Allan Quatermain (1887) to his own son Arthur, who had died tragically during its writing, giving Quatermain's death poignant personal gravity.

items.title: Quiz Q#1382 · H. Rider Haggard
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. Rider Haggard
items.stem: Published by Longmans in 1887 with illustrations by Charles Kerr, which sequel to King Solomon's Mines completed H. Rider Haggard's heroic African adventure cycle?
items.explanation: Allan Quatermain (1887) was celebrated for the epic defense of the stair by the Zulu warrior Umslopogaas and the tragic death of Allan Quatermain.

items.title: Quiz Q#1383 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: Which 1876 volume of verse translations from French Romantic poets into English was the debut publication of Indian prodigy Toru Dutt, praised by Edmund Gosse in the Saturday Review?
options: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields
items.explanation: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields (1876) was published at the Saptahik Sambad Press in Bhowanipore, Calcutta, containing 165 translations from French poets including Victor Hugo and Baudelaire.

items.title: Quiz Q#1384 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: Printed in Calcutta in 1876 without a preface or publisher's name, which remarkable translation volume by twenty-year-old Toru Dutt prompted Edmund Gosse to hail her as a rare poetic genius?
options: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields
items.explanation: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields was discovered by Edmund Gosse, who was stunned that an Indian woman writing in English could render 19th-century French poetry with such lyrical finesse.

items.title: Quiz Q#1385 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: In which posthumously published 1879 French epistolary/diary novel by Toru Dutt does the devout young heroine Marguerite d'Arvers record her tragic love triangle with Gaston des Blais and Louis Lefèvre?
options: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields
items.explanation: Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers (1879) was written in French by Toru Dutt and published posthumously in Paris under the editorship of Clarisse Bader, making Dutt the first Indian author to publish a novel in French.

items.title: Quiz Q#1386 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: Which bilingual 19th-century Indian woman of letters authored the French novel Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers (1879), discovered among her papers after her tragic death from tuberculosis at age twenty-one?
items.explanation: Toru Dutt (1856–1877) died at just twenty-one, leaving behind groundbreaking works in both English and French that bridged Indian, French, and Victorian English literary traditions.

items.title: Quiz Q#1387 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: Published in Paris by Didier in 1879 with an introduction by French scholar Clarisse Bader, which work by Toru Dutt holds the distinction of being the first novel written in French by an Indian writer?
options: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields
Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
items.explanation: Le Journal de Mademoiselle d'Arvers (1879) is a sensitive psychological study of Catholic family life and tragic love in provincial France, composed by Toru Dutt during her stay in Europe.

items.title: Quiz Q#1388 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: In which 1882 posthumous poetry collection by Toru Dutt are Sanskrit epics transformed into English ballads, including 'Savitri', 'Lakshman', 'Dhruva', and the nostalgic masterpiece 'Our Casuarina Tree'?
options: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields
Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
items.explanation: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (1882) was published in London by Kegan Paul with an introductory memoir by Edmund Gosse, containing Dutt's magnificent ode 'Our Casuarina Tree'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1389 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: Which Indian poet composed the famous sonnet 'The Lotus', resolving the rivalry between the rose and the lily with the line: "Love came to Flora asking for a flower / That would of flowers be undisputed queen"?
items.explanation: Toru Dutt's sonnet 'The Lotus' appears in Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (1882), celebrating the lotus as the perfect flower blending the rose's red and the lily's white.

items.title: Quiz Q#1390 · Toru Dutt
items.stem: Published in London in 1882 with a critical introductory memoir by Edmund Gosse, which collection features Toru Dutt's celebrated personal lyric 'Our Casuarina Tree'?
options: A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields
Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan
items.explanation: Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan (1882) immortalized Toru Dutt in English literature. 'Our Casuarina Tree' compares the tree to a gigantic python and mourns her lost siblings Abju and Aru.

items.title: Quiz Q#1391 · George Gissing
items.stem: In which 1889 naturalistic novel by George Gissing does Michael Snowdon attempt to train his impoverished granddaughter Jane as an apostle of philanthropy in the squalid slums of Clerkenwell?
items.explanation: The Nether World (1889) is George Gissing's grimmest naturalistic novel of London working-class poverty, depicting the cruel economic realities that crush Jane Snowdon and Sidney Kirkwood.

items.title: Quiz Q#1392 · George Gissing
items.stem: Published in three volumes by Smith, Elder in 1889, which unsparingly pessimistic novel by George Gissing presents a devastating documentary portrait of Victorian slum degradation in London's East End?
items.explanation: The Nether World (1889) closed Gissing's early cycle of working-class novels, presenting the slums of Clerkenwell as a modern inferno devoid of spiritual hope or economic escape.

items.title: Quiz Q#1393 · George Gissing
items.stem: In which 1891 masterpiece by George Gissing does the uncommercial, high-minded novelist Edwin Reardon slowly starve in literary poverty while his cynical rival Jasper Milvain prospers through hack journalism?
items.explanation: New Grub Street (1891) is Gissing's greatest novel, dissecting the commercialization of Victorian literary culture and the tragedy of Edwin Reardon, Alfred Yule, and Marian Yule.

items.title: Quiz Q#1394 · George Gissing
items.stem: Published in three volumes in 1891, which novel by George Gissing provides an uncompromising, autobiographical exposé of the commodification of literature and the struggles of writers in late-Victorian London?
items.explanation: New Grub Street (1891) drew upon Gissing's own harrowing experiences of literary poverty, contrasting the brutal market pressures of the reading public with sincere artistic creation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1395 · George Gissing
items.stem: In which 1893 New Woman novel by George Gissing does the independent Rhoda Nunn establish an office to train 'surplus' unmarried women for clerical careers, fiercely resisting marriage as an enslaving trap?
items.explanation: The Odd Women (1893) examines Victorian Britain's 'redundant women'—the half-million surplus unmarried females identified in the 1851 census—through Rhoda Nunn and the tragic Madden sisters.

items.title: Quiz Q#1396 · George Gissing
items.stem: Addressing the Victorian social problem of half a million unmarried 'surplus' women identified by contemporary census reports, which 1893 novel was written by George Gissing?
items.explanation: The Odd Women (1893) was published by Lawrence and Bullen, celebrated for its complex feminist debates on female economic independence, marriage, and female autonomy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1397 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In which 1895 debut novel by Joseph Conrad does the Dutch merchant Kaspar Almayer harbor delusional dreams of diamond wealth along the Pantai River in Borneo, only to be abandoned by his daughter Nina?
items.explanation: Almayer's Folly: A Story of an Eastern River (1895) was Joseph Conrad's first novel, introducing the ruined trader Kaspar Almayer in the fictional Malayan settlement of Sambir.

items.title: Quiz Q#1398 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Written between 1889 and 1894 while the author served as a merchant seaman and published in April 1895 by T. Fisher Unwin, which was Joseph Conrad's debut literary work?
items.explanation: Almayer's Folly launched Conrad's literary career at age thirty-seven. Edward Garnett recognized its exceptional stylistic power, encouraging Conrad to leave the sea and become a full-time author.

items.title: Quiz Q#1399 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In which 1896 second novel by Joseph Conrad does the disgraced clerk Peter Willems betray his benefactor Captain Lingard and lead tribal enemies to the secret river settlement in Borneo?
items.explanation: An Outcast of the Islands (1896) serves as a prequel to Almayer's Folly, tracing Peter Willems's moral degradation and his obsessive, destructive passion for the native woman Aïssa.

items.title: Quiz Q#1400 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1896, which second Malayan novel by Joseph Conrad confirmed his reputation as an extraordinary stylist of imperial corruption and psychological exile?
items.explanation: An Outcast of the Islands (1896) consolidated Conrad's 'Lingard Trilogy' (along with Almayer's Folly and The Rescue), showcasing his brooding existential vision of the tropics.

items.title: Quiz Q#1401 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In which 1899 modernist novella by Joseph Conrad does the sailor Charles Marlow travel aboard a steamship up the Congo River to retrieve the ivory trader Kurtz, who has established a godlike reign of terror?
items.explanation: Heart of Darkness (1899) explores Marlow's nightmarish voyage into the Belgian Congo, confronting Kurtz's moral disintegration and the horrific reality of European imperialist exploitation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1402 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Which haunting dying words are gasped by the ivory trader Kurtz at the climax of Joseph Conrad's 1899 novella Heart of Darkness: "The horror! The horror!"?
items.explanation: Kurtz's final whisper—'The horror! The horror!'—in Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (1899) represents his terrifying moment of supreme moral clarity regarding his own soul and imperial savagery.

items.title: Quiz Q#1403 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Serialized in Blackwood's Magazine in 1899 to celebrate the journal's thousandth issue and collected in Youth (1902), which work by Joseph Conrad is a supreme masterpiece of psychological and political modernism?
items.explanation: Heart of Darkness was published in Blackwood's ('Maga') from February to April 1899, based on Conrad's own harrowing 1890 voyage to the Congo Free State aboard the Roi des Belges.

items.title: Quiz Q#1404 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In which 1900 novel by Joseph Conrad does the idealistic young first mate Jim abandon the damaged pilgrim ship Patna in a moment of panic, spending the rest of his life seeking redemption in the remote Malayan territory of Patusan?
items.explanation: Lord Jim (1900) follows Jim's lifelong quest to recover his lost romantic self-image after his cowardice aboard the Patna, narrated largely by Charles Marlow.

items.title: Quiz Q#1405 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Serialized in Blackwood's Magazine between October 1899 and November 1900, which novel by Joseph Conrad uses Marlow's sophisticated, shifting narrative perspective to investigate the nature of honor and courage?
items.explanation: Lord Jim (1900) expanded from a planned short story into a complex modernist novel, exploring how a single moment of psychological failure shatters Jim's romantic heroic ideals.

items.title: Quiz Q#1406 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: In which 1904 political masterpiece by Joseph Conrad is the incorruptible Italian sailor Giovanni Battista Fidanza ('Nostromo') tasked with saving the silver of the San Tomé mine in the fictional South American republic of Costaguana?
items.explanation: Nostromo: A Tale of the Seaboard (1904) is Conrad's epic political novel set in Costaguana, exploring the corrupting power of 'material interests' (the silver mine) on individuals and revolutionary politics.

items.title: Quiz Q#1407 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Which Anglo-Polish novelist composed the panoramic political epic Nostromo (1904), meditating on political revolution, capitalist imperialism, and the grim psychological truth that: "Action is consolatory. It is the enemy of thought"?
items.explanation: Joseph Conrad wrote Nostromo during eighteen months of intense creative agony, constructing the fictional state of Costaguana as an epic microcosm of global capitalism.

items.title: Quiz Q#1408 · Joseph Conrad
items.stem: Subtitled 'A Tale of the Seaboard' and set around the Golfo Placido in the fictional republic of Costaguana, which 1904 novel is widely regarded as Joseph Conrad's greatest political and narrative triumph?
items.explanation: Nostromo (1904) was published by Harper & Brothers. F. R. Leavis famously included Conrad in The Great Tradition primarily on the strength of Nostromo and The Secret Agent.

items.title: Quiz Q#1409 · A. E. Housman
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · A. E. Housman
items.stem: In which 1896 collection of sixty-three pastoral lyrics by A. E. Housman does an idealized young rural persona meditate on early death, military duty, and the loss of youth?
items.explanation: A Shropshire Lad (1896) is A. E. Housman's classic volume of melancholy lyrics set in a semi-imaginary Shropshire, including 'Loveliest of trees, the cherry now' and 'To an Athlete Dying Young'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1410 · A. E. Housman
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · A. E. Housman
items.stem: Which Victorian classical scholar and poet opened the second lyric of A Shropshire Lad with the celebrated spring lines: "Loveliest of trees, the cherry now / Is hung with bloom along the bough, / And stands about the woodland ride / Wearing white for Eastertide"?
items.explanation: A. E. Housman (1859–1936) published 'Loveliest of trees' in A Shropshire Lad (1896), calculating his remaining fifty years of life to enjoy the transient beauty of cherry blossoms.

items.title: Quiz Q#1411 · A. E. Housman
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · A. E. Housman
items.stem: Published at the author's own expense by Kegan Paul in 1896 after being rejected by multiple publishers, which volume became an enormous cultural phenomenon during the Boer War and World War I?
items.explanation: A Shropshire Lad (1896) achieved immense popularity among British soldiers in the trenches of World War I, capturing the poignant transience of youth and stoic defiance in simple ballad meters.

items.title: Quiz Q#1412 · A. E. Housman
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · A. E. Housman
items.stem: In which 1922 collection—the only other poetry volume published during the author's lifetime—did A. E. Housman include his famous 'Epitaph on an Army of Mercenaries'?
items.explanation: Last Poems (1922) was published by Grant Richards, containing forty-one lyrics composed mostly during the same fertile creative period (1895–1910) as A Shropshire Lad.

items.title: Quiz Q#1413 · A. E. Housman
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · A. E. Housman
items.stem: Who is the poet who honored the British professional soldiers of the British Expeditionary Force in his famous 'Epitaph on an Army of Mercenaries', concluding: "Their shoulders held the sky suspended; / They stood, and earth's foundations stay; / What God abandoned, these defended, / And saved the sum of things for pay"?
items.explanation: A. E. Housman composed this magnificent tribute in Last Poems (1922) to honor the British professional soldiers who held the line against overwhelming German forces at Ypres in 1914.

items.title: Quiz Q#1414 · A. E. Housman
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · A. E. Housman
items.stem: Published in London in 1922 when the author was Kennedy Professor of Latin at Cambridge, which volume was A. E. Housman's final self-curated collection of verse?
items.explanation: Last Poems (1922) was an immediate commercial success, selling over 20,000 copies in its first months and confirming Housman's enduring mastery of the classical English lyric.

items.title: Quiz Q#1415 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
