items.stem: In which 1887 detective novel does Arthur Conan Doyle first introduce Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John H. Watson as prospective flatmates at 221B Baker Street?
items.explanation: A Study in Scarlet (1887) is the historic debut of Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson, introducing Holmes's 'science of deduction' in solving the murder of Enoch Drebber.

items.title: Quiz Q#1416 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: In which detective story does Sherlock Holmes astound Dr. Watson upon their very first meeting at St. Bartholomew's Hospital with the famous deduction: "You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive"?
items.explanation: Sherlock Holmes demonstrates his powers of observational deduction immediately upon meeting Watson in Chapter 1 of Arthur Conan Doyle's A Study in Scarlet (1887).

items.title: Quiz Q#1417 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: First published in Beeton's Christmas Annual for November 1887, which short novel introduced the world's most famous consulting detective, Sherlock Holmes?
items.explanation: A Study in Scarlet was bought by Ward, Lock & Co. for just £25 and published in Beeton's Christmas Annual in 1887, marking the birth of the Sherlock Holmes canon.

items.title: Quiz Q#1418 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: In which 1890 detective novel by Arthur Conan Doyle does Sherlock Holmes solve the mystery of the stolen Agra treasure and the death of Bartholomew Sholto, while Dr. Watson falls in love with Mary Morstan?
items.explanation: The Sign of the Four (1890) involves Jonathan Small, the Andaman islander Tonga, and the secret pact of four convicts in colonial India, concluding with Watson's engagement to Mary Morstan.

items.title: Quiz Q#1419 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: Commissioned at a famous London dinner hosted by Lippincott's Monthly Magazine editor J. M. Stoddart in August 1889—which simultaneously produced Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray—which second Holmes novel was written by Arthur Conan Doyle?
items.explanation: The Sign of the Four was published in Lippincott's in February 1890 after Stoddart commissioned both Conan Doyle and Oscar Wilde at a historic dinner at the Langham Hotel.

items.title: Quiz Q#1420 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: In which 1892 collection of twelve short stories by Arthur Conan Doyle does the female opera singer Irene Adler outwit Sherlock Holmes in the opening case, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'?
items.explanation: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1892) collects twelve classic stories published in The Strand Magazine, opening with 'A Scandal in Bohemia' where Irene Adler is forever remembered as 'the woman'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1421 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: Which Victorian author created the detective who famously lectures his companion on the difference between passive seeing and active deduction: "You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear"?
items.explanation: Sherlock Holmes explains the foundation of his deductive method to Dr. Watson in 'A Scandal in Bohemia', the opening story of The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1892).

items.title: Quiz Q#1422 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: Illustrated with the famous Sidney Paget drawings in The Strand Magazine between July 1891 and June 1892, which volume transformed Sherlock Holmes into an international cultural icon?
items.explanation: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1892) published by George Newnes established the formula of the self-contained monthly magazine detective story, illustrated indelibly by Sidney Paget.

items.title: Quiz Q#1423 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: In which 1894 story collection by Arthur Conan Doyle does Sherlock Holmes introduce his brilliant older brother Mycroft ('The Greek Interpreter') and confront Professor James Moriarty at the Reichenbach Falls?
items.explanation: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes (1894) contains eleven stories, culminating in 'The Final Problem' where Holmes seemingly plunges to his death battling Professor Moriarty.

items.title: Quiz Q#1424 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: In which Sherlock Holmes story does Holmes describe his criminal nemesis Professor James Moriarty as "the Napoleon of crime... the organizer of half that is evil and of nearly all that is undetected in this great city"?
items.explanation: Holmes introduces Professor Moriarty in 'The Final Problem', published in The Strand in December 1893 and collected in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes (1894).

items.title: Quiz Q#1425 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: Concluding with 'The Final Problem'—in which Conan Doyle attempted to kill off his famous detective at Switzerland's Reichenbach Falls—which volume was published in 1894?
items.explanation: Conan Doyle killed Holmes in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes (1894) to concentrate on historical novels, but public mourning and financial offers eventually forced him to revive the detective.

items.title: Quiz Q#1426 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: In which 1901–1902 gothic mystery novel by Arthur Conan Doyle do Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to the desolate Devonshire moors of Dartmoor to investigate a demonic spectral hound haunting Sir Henry Baskerville?
items.explanation: The Hound of the Baskervilles (1902) is Conan Doyle's most celebrated full-length novel, featuring the atmospheric Grimpen Mire, the naturalist Stapleton, and the phosphorous-painted hound.

items.title: Quiz Q#1427 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: Which famous piece of dialogue occurs in Arthur Conan Doyle's The Hound of the Baskervilles when Dr. Mortimer whispers to Holmes: "Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!"?
items.explanation: Dr. Mortimer's chilling disclosure in Chapter 2 of The Hound of the Baskervilles (1902) establishes the supernatural terror surrounding the sudden death of Sir Charles Baskerville.

items.title: Quiz Q#1428 · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Arthur Conan Doyle
items.stem: Serialized in The Strand Magazine between August 1901 and April 1902 to ecstatic public acclaim, which was the first Sherlock Holmes story to appear after Holmes's apparent death in 'The Final Problem'?
items.explanation: Conan Doyle set The Hound of the Baskervilles before the events of 'The Final Problem', avoiding a resurrection of Holmes until 'The Adventure of the Empty House' in 1903.

items.title: Quiz Q#1429 · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.stem: In which 1893 debut collection of psychological short stories by George Egerton (Mary Chavelita Dunne) does the opening story 'A Cross Line' candidly portray a married woman's complex erotic daydreams and inner independence?
items.explanation: Keynotes (1893) was George Egerton's sensational debut. 'A Cross Line' was celebrated for its radical, poetic exploration of female sexual desire and psychological complexity.

items.title: Quiz Q#1430 · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.stem: Which Anglo-Irish New Woman writer and translator of Knut Hamsun wrote the groundbreaking 1893 collection Keynotes under the male pseudonym George Egerton?
items.explanation: Mary Chavelita Dunne (1859–1945) adopted the pen name George Egerton. Her impressionistic, Scandinavian-influenced prose introduced proto-modernist psychological interiority to British fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1431 · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.stem: Published by John Lane at the Bodley Head in 1893 with cover and title-page designs by Aubrey Beardsley, which collection gave its name to the famous fin-de-siècle 'Keynotes Series' of avant-garde literature?
items.explanation: Keynotes was an enormous critical and commercial success, leading publisher John Lane to launch the celebrated 'Keynotes Series' of cutting-edge aesthetic and New Woman fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1432 · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.stem: In which 1894 companion collection to Keynotes did George Egerton present darker, harsher stories of female entrapment, domestic violence, alcoholism, and disillusioned marriage?
items.explanation: Discords (1894) followed Keynotes, offering realistic, unsparing portraits of women's physical and emotional suffering in stories like 'A Psychological Moment' and 'Wedlock'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1433 · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.stem: Which fin-de-siècle feminist writer followed her successful 1893 collection Keynotes with the darker, realistic volume Discords (1894), exploring the biological and economic traps of Victorian womanhood?
items.explanation: George Egerton's Discords (1894) reinforced her reputation as one of the boldest stylists of the 1890s, using lyrical, stream-of-consciousness techniques to explore female anger.

items.title: Quiz Q#1434 · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · George Egerton / Mary Chavelita Dunne
items.stem: Published in London in 1894 by John Lane with cover art by Aubrey Beardsley, which short story collection confirmed George Egerton as one of the central figures of late-Victorian Decadence and New Woman writing?
items.explanation: Discords was published in December 1894 in the Keynotes Series, cementing Egerton's prominence alongside other Bodley Head luminaries like Arthur Symons and Ernest Dowson.

items.title: Quiz Q#1435 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: In which 1912 collection of prose poetry does Rabindranath Tagore offer humble devotional songs to the Divine, opening with the famous prayer: "Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again..."?
items.explanation: Gitanjali: Song Offerings (1912) was Tagore's English prose translation of his devotional Bengali songs, praised by W. B. Yeats in his celebrated Introduction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1436 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: In the English Gitanjali, which poem famously articulates the singer's humble spiritual surrender: "I am here to sing thee songs. In this hall of thine I have a corner seat. In thy world I have no work to do; my useless life can only break out in tunes..."?
items.explanation: Poem 15 of English Gitanjali (1912) embodies Tagore's mystical aesthetic of singing songs in divine adoration as the supreme purpose of human existence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1437 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: First printed in November 1912 by the India Society of London with an enthusiastic introductory essay by W. B. Yeats, which volume directly earned Rabindranath Tagore the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature?
items.explanation: Gitanjali: Song Offerings (1912) caused an international sensation in literary London, making Tagore the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.

items.title: Quiz Q#1438 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: In which 1910 original Bengali poetry collection did Rabindranath Tagore compose the 157 devotional and philosophical songs of spiritual longing that formed the basis of his later world-renowned English volume?
items.explanation: The original Bengali Gitanjali was published in Calcutta in August 1910, written during a period of personal bereavement following the deaths of his wife, son, and daughter.

items.title: Quiz Q#1439 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: Published in Calcutta in August 1910, which original Bengali volume contains Tagore's celebrated patriotic prayer 'Chitto Jetha Bhayshunyo' (translated into English as 'Where the mind is without fear')?
items.explanation: The Bengali Gitanjali (1910) contains Poem 72, which Tagore translated in the English collection as Poem 35: 'Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free...'

items.title: Quiz Q#1440 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: In which 1916 novel by Rabindranath Tagore (translated into English in 1919) is the heroine Bimala torn between the moderate, moral cosmopolitanism of her husband Nikhilesh and the fiery, destructive Swadeshi nationalism of Sandip?
items.explanation: The Home and the World (Ghare Baire, 1916) explores the 1905 Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi movement through the conflicting diary entries of Bimala, Nikhilesh, and Sandip.

items.title: Quiz Q#1441 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: Constructed through three interlocking first-person diary narratives, which 1916 political novel by Rabindranath Tagore critiques xenophobic militant nationalism in favor of universal humanism?
items.explanation: The Home and the World (1916) presented Tagore's profound warning against fanaticism, demonstrating how violent Swadeshi boycotts harmed impoverished Muslim tenants and divided the community.

items.title: Quiz Q#1442 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: Which Nobel laureate opened his celebrated 1912 English collection with the immortal prayer of spiritual infinity: "Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life"?
items.explanation: Song 1 of Rabindranath Tagore's Gitanjali: Song Offerings (1912) expresses the soul's infinite capacity to receive divine grace through continuous renewal.

items.title: Quiz Q#1443 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: Published in London in November 1912 in a limited edition of 750 copies by the India Society before Macmillan issued its popular trade edition in March 1913, which work introduced Tagore to the Western world?
items.explanation: Gitanjali: Song Offerings (1912) was sponsored by the India Society, featuring a frontispiece sketch by William Rothenstein and Yeats's memorable praise.

items.title: Quiz Q#1444 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: Published by Macmillan in 1913 shortly after his Nobel Prize announcement, which collection of lyrics by Rabindranath Tagore was subtitled 'Lyrics of Love and Life', presenting human romantic passion as an aspect of divine love?
items.explanation: The Gardener (1913) was Tagore's second English volume with Macmillan, translating his earlier Bengali love poetry from collections like Kshanika and Chaitali.

items.title: Quiz Q#1445 · Rabindranath Tagore
items.stem: Translated into English by Surendranath Tagore and published in London by Macmillan in 1919, which novel by Rabindranath Tagore was adapted into a celebrated 1984 film by Satyajit Ray?
options: The Home and the World (English translation)
items.explanation: The Home and the World (1919) was translated by Tagore's nephew Surendranath Tagore. Satyajit Ray's 1984 cinematic adaptation Ghare Baire won international critical acclaim.

items.title: Quiz Q#1446 · Krupabai Satthianadhan
items.stem: In which 1887 autobiographical novel by Krupabai Satthianadhan does the young Indian Christian heroine Saguna defy orthodox social conventions to pursue higher education and medical studies in colonial Madras?
options: Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life
Love and Life Behind the Purdah
items.explanation: Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life (1887–1888) is Krupabai Satthianadhan's autobiographical novel, celebrating an Indian woman's intellectual empowerment and medical training.

items.title: Quiz Q#1447 · Krupabai Satthianadhan
items.stem: Which pioneering 19th-century Indian woman novelist, who was among the first Indian women to study medicine at Madras Medical College, authored the autobiographical novel Saguna?
items.explanation: Krupabai Satthianadhan (1862–1894) was a pioneering Indian feminist writer whose novels Saguna and Kamala explored female education and the inner lives of Indian women.

items.title: Quiz Q#1448 · Krupabai Satthianadhan
items.stem: Serialized in the Madras Christian College Magazine between 1887 and 1888 before its book publication in 1895, which work is recognized as the first autobiographical novel written in English by an Indian woman?
options: Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life
items.explanation: Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life holds historical significance as the earliest full-length autobiographical novel in English by an Indian woman writer.

items.title: Quiz Q#1449 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which 1901 colonial picaresque masterpiece by Rudyard Kipling does the orphaned Irish boy Kimball O'Hara wander across northern India along the Grand Trunk Road as the chela to a Tibetan lama while working for the British Secret Service?
items.explanation: Kim (1901) is Kipling's panoramic masterpiece set in India, interweaving Kim's spiritual quest for the River of the Arrow with the Teshoo Lama and his espionage duties in 'The Great Game'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1450 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Which British imperial author created the young Irish street boy in Lahore known affectionately among Indians as "Little Friend of all the World"?
items.explanation: Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay and achieved world renown with works celebrating British India, winning the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

items.title: Quiz Q#1451 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Published in 1901 with illustrations by the author's father, John Lockwood Kipling, which novel is celebrated for its vivid, sympathetic panorama of Indian railway culture, bazaars, and religions along the Grand Trunk Road?
items.explanation: Kim (1901) was hailed by Nirad C. Chaudhuri as the finest story about India in English, capturing the immense diversity of northern India with sensory brilliance.

items.title: Quiz Q#1452 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Published in Lahore in 1886 while the author was working as assistant editor of the Civil and Military Gazette, which collection of satirical verse was Rudyard Kipling's first published book?
items.explanation: Departmental Ditties and Other Verses (1886) was Kipling's debut, packaged initially to look like an official government docket, satirizing Anglo-Indian bureaucratic life in Simla.

items.title: Quiz Q#1453 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which 1888 collection of forty short stories by Rudyard Kipling does the opening tale 'Lispeth' recount the betrayal of a Pahari hill girl who rescues a wounded Englishman at Kotgarh?
items.explanation: Plain Tales from the Hills (1888) collected Kipling's early journalistic stories written for the Civil and Military Gazette, depicting the social scandals and racial tensions of Simla.

items.title: Quiz Q#1454 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: First published in Calcutta in 1888 by Thacker, Spink & Co., which volume introduced Rudyard Kipling's famous recurring soldier trio—Privates Mulvaney, Ortheris, and Learoyd?
items.explanation: Plain Tales from the Hills (1888) launched Kipling's British reputation, acclaimed for its crisp journalistic brevity and insider knowledge of colonial Anglo-Indian life.

items.title: Quiz Q#1455 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which 1892 poetry collection by Rudyard Kipling do common British soldiers ('Tommy Atkins') narrate their experiences of colonial warfare in vernacular Cockney dialect, including 'Gunga Din' and 'Mandalay'?
items.explanation: Barrack-Room Ballads and Other Verses (1892) gave voice to the British enlisted soldier, celebrating his courage, slang, and rough humor in the outposts of the British Empire.

items.title: Quiz Q#1456 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Which famous poem from Rudyard Kipling's 1892 Barrack-Room Ballads concludes with the British soldier's humble tribute to the Indian water-bearer: "An' for all 'is dirty 'ide / 'E was white, clean white inside / When 'e went to tend the wounded under fire!... / You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din!"?
items.explanation: Kipling's 'Gunga Din' in Barrack-Room Ballads (1892) immortalized the selfless heroism of the Indian bhisti (water-carrier) serving the British army in frontier campaigns.

items.title: Quiz Q#1457 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Published in 1892 by Methuen in London, which collection established Rudyard Kipling as the undisputed poetic bard of British imperial soldiers and working-class military life?
items.explanation: Barrack-Room Ballads was an international bestseller in 1892, containing iconic recitation pieces like 'Danny Deever', 'Fuzzy-Wuzzy', 'Gunga Din', and 'Mandalay'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1458 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which 1894 classic by Rudyard Kipling is the feral human child Mowgli raised by the Seeonee wolf pack under the protection of the black panther Bagheera and the brown bear Baloo?
items.explanation: The Jungle Book (1894) introduces Mowgli, the tiger Shere Khan, Kaa the python, and the famous 'Law of the Jungle', alongside stories like 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1459 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Which Victorian author composed The Jungle Book (1894), where the animals of the jungle greet each other with the sacred Master-Word of peace: "We be of one blood, ye and I"?
items.explanation: Rudyard Kipling wrote The Jungle Book while living in Brattleboro, Vermont, drawing on Indian wildlife and ancient fables from the Panchatantra.

items.title: Quiz Q#1460 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Published in 1894 with illustrations by John Lockwood Kipling and others, which work features the heroic mongoose Rikki-Tikki-Tavi fighting the cobras Nag and Nagaina in an Indian bungalow garden?
items.explanation: The Jungle Book (1894) contains seven stories, each paired with verse, including 'Mowgli's Brothers', 'Kaa's Hunting', 'The White Seal', and 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1461 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which 1895 sequel by Rudyard Kipling does the adolescent Mowgli defend the Seeonee pack from the terrifying invasion of the red dogs (Dholes) of the Deccan, before finally leaving the jungle for human society?
items.explanation: The Second Jungle Book (1895) concludes Mowgli's education with 'Red Dog' and 'The Spring Running', where eighteen-year-old Mowgli tearfully bids farewell to the jungle.

items.title: Quiz Q#1462 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Which 1895 collection by Rudyard Kipling contains the poem 'The Law of the Jungle', setting out the famous pack law: "Now this is the Law of the Jungle—as old and as true as the sky; / And the Wolf that shall keep it may prosper, but the Wolf that shall break it must die"?
items.explanation: The poem 'The Law of the Jungle' was published in The Second Jungle Book (1895), emphasizing communal solidarity: 'the strength of the Pack is the Wolf, and the strength of the Wolf is the Pack'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1463 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Published in 1895 by Macmillan, which book completes Rudyard Kipling's animal fables, featuring 'The King's Ankus' and the Arctic story 'Quiquern'?
items.explanation: The Second Jungle Book (1895) was composed in Vermont, deepening Kipling's mythic vision of animal society, ancient treasures, and human destiny.

items.title: Quiz Q#1464 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which 1896 poetry collection by Rudyard Kipling does an elderly Scottish marine engineer deliver the dramatic monologue 'McAndrew's Hymn', discovering divine cosmic harmony in the steam engines of ocean liners?
items.explanation: The Seven Seas (1896) collected Kipling's maritime and imperial poetry, celebrated for 'McAndrew's Hymn' which turned industrial machinery and marine engines into sacred poetry.

items.title: Quiz Q#1465 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Which Victorian poet celebrated the steam-driven machinery of the British Empire in The Seven Seas (1896), singing of ocean liners: "The Liner she's a lady, an' she walks on in collar an' curls— / The Man-o'-War's 'er 'usband, an' 'e conquers all the worlds"?
items.explanation: Rudyard Kipling published 'The Liner She's a Lady' in The Seven Seas (1896), personifying British passenger liners and royal naval warships as the masters of world trade.

items.title: Quiz Q#1466 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Published in London and New York in 1896, which poetry collection by Rudyard Kipling included major maritime poems like 'The 'Mary Gloster'' and 'The Song of the Banjo'?
items.explanation: The Seven Seas (1896) confirmed Kipling's status as the poet laureate of the British Empire and the industrial mariner, exploring global sea lanes and naval supremacy.

items.title: Quiz Q#1467 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: In which 1897 coming-of-age novel by Rudyard Kipling is spoiled fifteen-year-old American millionaire's son Harvey Cheyne swept overboard from an ocean liner and rescued by the fishing schooner We're Here?
items.explanation: Captains Courageous (1897) depicts Harvey Cheyne's moral regeneration through disciplined manual labor alongside the Portuguese fisherman Manuel on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland.

items.title: Quiz Q#1468 · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Set among the cod-fishing fleets of the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, which 1897 seafaring novel was Rudyard Kipling's only full-length work set in North America?
items.explanation: Captains Courageous (1897) drew on Kipling's residence in Gloucester, Massachusetts, praised for its documentary accuracy regarding the hazardous North Atlantic fishing trade.

items.title: Quiz Q#1469 · Beatrix Potter
items.stem: In which 1902 children's classic by Beatrix Potter does a disobedient young rabbit in a blue jacket squeeze under the gate into Mr. McGregor's garden, losing his coat and shoes?
items.explanation: The Tale of Peter Rabbit (1902) was Beatrix Potter's first published book, following Peter Rabbit's perilous adventure in Mr. McGregor's vegetable patch.

items.title: Quiz Q#1470 · Beatrix Potter
items.stem: Which Victorian/Edwardian children's author opened her famous story with Old Mrs. Rabbit warning: "Now, my dears, you may go into the fields or down the lane, but don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden: your Father had an accident there; he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor"?
items.explanation: Beatrix Potter (1866–1943) invented Peter Rabbit in an illustrated letter sent in September 1893 to Noel Moore, the five-year-old son of her former governess.

items.title: Quiz Q#1471 · Beatrix Potter
items.stem: Originally privately printed by the author in December 1901 before being published in color by Frederick Warne & Co. in October 1902, which classic began Beatrix Potter's legendary series of 'little books'?
items.explanation: The Tale of Peter Rabbit was turned down by six publishers until Potter printed 250 copies herself; Warne then agreed to publish it if she re-did the illustrations in color, selling 20,000 copies immediately.

items.title: Quiz Q#1472 · Cornelia Sorabji
items.stem: In which 1901 short story collection by Cornelia Sorabji—the first Indian woman to study law at Oxford—are the secluded lives, joys, and domestic tragedies of purdahnashin (veiled) women depicted from an insider's legal perspective?
options: Love and Life Behind the Purdah
items.explanation: Love and Life Behind the Purdah (1901) was Cornelia Sorabji's pioneering collection of stories, revealing the legal, emotional, and social conditions of women secluded behind the veil in India.

items.title: Quiz Q#1473 · Cornelia Sorabji
items.stem: Published in London in 1901 with introductory essays by the Marchioness of Dufferin and Ava and Lord Hobhouse, which landmark book was written by Cornelia Sorabji to advocate for the legal rights of secluded Indian women?
options: Love and Life Behind the Purdah
items.explanation: Cornelia Sorabji (1866–1954) was appointed Legal Adviser to the Court of Wards in Bengal, using her literary writings like Love and Life Behind the Purdah (1901) to support purdahnashin women.

items.title: Quiz Q#1474 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: In which 1895 science-fiction masterpiece by H. G. Wells does the Time Traveller journey to the year 802,701 AD to discover that humanity has evolved into two degenerate species—the gentle, childlike Eloi and the subterranean, carnivorous Morlocks?
items.explanation: The Time Machine (1895) was H. G. Wells's revolutionary debut 'scientific romance', using evolutionary theory and thermodynamic entropy to satirize Victorian class division.

items.title: Quiz Q#1475 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: Evolving from an earlier student sketch titled 'The Chronic Argonauts' published in the Science Schools Journal, which 1895 novella by H. G. Wells coined the term 'time machine' and launched the modern time-travel genre?
options: The First Men in the Moon
items.explanation: The Time Machine was serialized in W. E. Henley's New Review in 1895 before Heinemann published the book, establishing Wells as a pioneer of modern science fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1476 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: In which 1896 scientific romance by H. G. Wells is the shipwrecked gentleman Edward Prendick rescued by the sinister scientist Moreau, who conducts painful vivisection experiments to transform animals into humanoid 'Beast Folk'?
items.explanation: The Island of Doctor Moreau (1896) explores Dr. Moreau's sadistic attempts to sculpt animals into men on Noble's Isle, bound by the recitation of the Law: 'Not to go on all-Fours; that is the Law. Are we not Men?'

items.title: Quiz Q#1477 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: Engaging directly with Victorian anxieties over vivisection, degeneration, and Darwinian animal ancestry, which 1896 novel by H. G. Wells features the horrific 'House of Pain'?
items.explanation: The Island of Doctor Moreau (1896) challenged Victorian human exceptionalism, demonstrating how the surgically constructed Beast Folk inevitably revert to animal savagery.

items.title: Quiz Q#1478 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: In which 1897 scientific romance by H. G. Wells does the albino optics researcher Griffin discover a formula to make human tissue invisible, terrorizing the Sussex village of Iping in a megalomaniacal 'Reign of Terror'?
items.explanation: The Invisible Man (1897) traces Griffin's descent into madness and isolation. Driven by power lust, he attempts to enlist Dr. Kemp before being hunted down and beaten to death by a crowd.

items.title: Quiz Q#1479 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: Serialized in Pearson's Weekly in 1897 before its book publication by C. Arthur Pearson, which novel by H. G. Wells warns against scientific intellect divorced from moral empathy?
options: The First Men in the Moon
items.explanation: The Invisible Man: A Grotesque Romance (1897) is Wells's cautionary tale of scientific hubris, as Griffin discovers that physical invisibility brings cold, hunger, and paranoia rather than absolute freedom.

items.title: Quiz Q#1480 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: In which 1898 apocalyptic novel by H. G. Wells do octopus-like Martians in towering tripod fighting-machines invade Victorian Surrey and London with Heat-Rays and Black Smoke, only to be slain by earthly bacteria?
options: The First Men in the Moon
items.explanation: The War of the Worlds (1898) depicts the Martian invasion of England, subverting British imperial complacency when the invaders are defeated not by military power but by microscopic bacteria.

items.title: Quiz Q#1481 · H. G. Wells
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · H. G. Wells
items.stem: Serialized in Pearson's Magazine in 1897 with illustrations by Warwick Goble, which 1898 invasion novel by H. G. Wells famously turned Victorian British imperialism upon itself, asking readers to imagine how Tasmanians felt during British colonization?
items.explanation: The War of the Worlds opened with Wells comparing the ruthless Martian invasion of Earth to the European extermination of the Tasmanian Aborigines, pioneering modern alien-invasion fiction.

items.title: Quiz Q#1482 · Mahatma Gandhi
items.stem: In which foundational 1909 dialogue did Mahatma Gandhi formulate his radical critique of modern industrial civilization and define true swaraj as self-rule and self-control, using a dialogue between the Editor and the Reader?
items.explanation: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule (1909) was written by Gandhi aboard the ship SS Kildonan Castle, defining Swaraj as moral self-mastery and introducing Satyagraha (soul-force).

items.title: Quiz Q#1483 · Mahatma Gandhi
items.stem: Which 20th-century leader and author asserted in his 1909 philosophical text Hind Swaraj that: "Real home-rule is self-rule or self-control... If we become free, India is free"?
items.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi composed Hind Swaraj (1909) in Gujarati, arguing that achieving political independence without moral transformation would simply reproduce 'English rule without the Englishman'.

items.title: Quiz Q#1484 · Mahatma Gandhi
items.stem: Written in Gujarati between 13 and 22 November 1909 aboard the ship Kildonan Castle and promptly banned by the British colonial government in Bombay, which work is Mahatma Gandhi's fundamental political manifesto?
items.explanation: Hind Swaraj was banned by the British authorities in March 1910 as seditious. Gandhi immediately translated it into English as Indian Home Rule to present his philosophy to the world.

items.title: Quiz Q#1485 · Mahatma Gandhi
items.stem: In which landmark autobiography did Mahatma Gandhi chronicle his childhood in Porbandar, legal education in London, civil-rights campaigns in South Africa, and spiritual experiments with vegetarianism and brahmacharya?
options: An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
items.explanation: The Story of My Experiments with Truth (1927–1929) is Gandhi's spiritual autobiography, translated from Gujarati by Mahadev Desai, chronicling his life up to the 1921 Nagpur Congress.

items.title: Quiz Q#1486 · Mahatma Gandhi
items.stem: Which world leader and moral thinker concluded his celebrated autobiography with the theological declaration: "There is no other God than Truth... and the only means for the realization of Truth is Ahimsa (non-violence)"?
items.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi's final chapter in The Story of My Experiments with Truth emphasizes that absolute devotion to Satya (Truth) is inseparable from the practice of universal love and Ahimsa.

items.title: Quiz Q#1487 · Mahatma Gandhi
items.stem: Serialized in weekly installments in Gandhi's journal Navajivan from 1925 to 1929 and translated into English by Mahadev Desai, which classic autobiography has been named among the most influential non-fiction books of the 20th century?
options: An Autobiography: The Story of My Experiments with Truth
items.explanation: The Story of My Experiments with Truth was composed while Gandhi was imprisoned at Yerwada Jail and published across 166 weekly chapters in Navajivan and Young India.

items.title: Quiz Q#1488 · Manmohan Ghose
items.stem: In which 1898 poetry collection did Indian poet and Oxford scholar Manmohan Ghose publish lyric poems in classical English forms, including 'The Kiss of Cupid' and 'April'?
items.explanation: Love Songs and Elegies (1898) was published by Elkin Mathews in London as part of the famous Shilling Garland series, establishing Manmohan Ghose's reputation as an exquisite English lyricist.

items.title: Quiz Q#1489 · Manmohan Ghose
items.stem: Published in London in 1898 by Elkin Mathews, which poetry volume was praised by Oscar Wilde and Laurence Binyon for bringing a delicate, classical English lyricism to fin-de-siècle verse?
items.explanation: Manmohan Ghose (1869–1924), older brother of Sri Aurobindo, was educated at Oxford alongside Laurence Binyon and Stephen Phillips. His Love Songs and Elegies was hailed by Oscar Wilde for its purity of English cadence.

items.title: Quiz Q#1490 · Algernon Charles Swinburne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Algernon Charles Swinburne
items.stem: In which controversial 1866 poem from Poems and Ballads does a pagan speaker mourn the death of the classical gods before the spread of Christianity, declaring: "Thou hast conquered, O pale Galilean; the world has grown grey from thy breath"?
items.explanation: 'Hymn to Proserpine' is Swinburne's dramatic monologue set in 363 AD during Emperor Julian's reign, lamenting the joyless asceticism of Christianity compared to classical pagan beauty.

items.title: Quiz Q#1491 · Algernon Charles Swinburne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Algernon Charles Swinburne
items.stem: Which Victorian poet caused a major literary scandal in 1866 with his pagan dirge 'Hymn to Proserpine', apostrophizing Christ with the famous line: "Thou hast conquered, O pale Galilean; the world has grown grey from thy breath"?
items.explanation: Algernon Charles Swinburne (1837–1909) scandalized Victorian Britain with Poems and Ballads (1866), celebrating pagan hedonism, anti-theism, and sensual musicality.

items.title: Quiz Q#1492 · Algernon Charles Swinburne
items.meta: The Nineteenth Century · Algernon Charles Swinburne
items.stem: Published by Edward Moxon in 1866 and withdrawn almost immediately under threat of prosecution for blasphemy and obscenity, which poetry collection by Swinburne featured 'Dolores', 'Laus Veneris', and 'The Garden of Proserpine'?
items.explanation: Poems and Ballads (First Series, 1866) was republished by John Camden Hotten after Moxon withdrew it, becoming a landmark of decadent, anti-Victorian poetic rebellion.

items.title: Quiz Q#1493 · Banjo Paterson
items.stem: In which famous 1890 Australian bush ballad by Banjo Paterson does an unnamed rider from the Snowy River on a small, mountain-bred pony outride the finest horsemen to recapture the wild colt from Old Regret?
items.explanation: 'The Man from Snowy River' (1890) is A. B. ('Banjo') Paterson's iconic Australian bush ballad, celebrating courage, horsemanship, and frontier spirit in the Snowy Mountains.

items.title: Quiz Q#1494 · Banjo Paterson
items.stem: Which Australian bush poet opened his celebrated narrative ballad with the thrilling lines: "There was movement at the station, for the word had passed around / That the colt from old Regret had got away..."?
items.explanation: Andrew Barton ('Banjo') Paterson (1864–1941) published 'The Man from Snowy River' in The Bulletin on 26 April 1890, capturing the popular imagination of the Australian nation.

items.title: Quiz Q#1495 · Banjo Paterson
items.stem: First printed in the Sydney Bulletin in April 1890 before becoming the title piece of an 1895 collection that sold over 100,000 copies, which ballad is a cornerstone of Australian national mythology?
items.explanation: The Man from Snowy River and Other Verses (1895) published by Angus & Robertson was one of the most successful books of poetry in English, surpassed in sales only by Kipling.

items.title: Quiz Q#1496 · Banjo Paterson
items.stem: In which 1895 Australian bush song by Banjo Paterson does an itinerant swagman camp by a billabong under the shade of a coolibah tree, steal a jumbuck, and drown himself in the waterhole rather than surrender to the troopers?
items.explanation: Waltzing Matilda (1895) is Australia's unofficial national anthem, recounting the defiant fate of the swagman whose ghost haunts the billabong.

items.title: Quiz Q#1497 · Banjo Paterson
items.stem: Which 19th-century Australian poet and balladist composed the lyrics to 'Waltzing Matilda' in 1895 while visiting Dagworth Station in Queensland with Christina Macpherson?
items.explanation: Banjo Paterson wrote the lyrics of 'Waltzing Matilda' to a Scottish tune played on the zither by Christina Macpherson, inspired by the bitter 1894 shearers' strike in Queensland.

items.title: Quiz Q#1498 · Banjo Paterson
items.stem: Composed in 1895 at Dagworth Station and first performed at the North Gregory Hotel in Winton, Queensland, which song is widely celebrated as the supreme folk anthem of Australian cultural identity?
items.explanation: Waltzing Matilda (1895) entered Australian folklore, combining distinct bush terminology (swagman, billabong, jumbuck, billy, squatter) with a spirit of anti-authoritarian rebellion.

items.title: Quiz Q#1499 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: In which 1895 novel by Thomas Hardy does the working-class stonemason Jude Fawley dream in vain of studying at Christminster University, while his unconventional relationship with his cousin Sue Bridehead ends in horrifying tragedy?
items.explanation: Jude the Obscure (1895) is Hardy's tragic masterpiece exploring thwarted educational aspirations, social class hostility, and marital misery through Jude and Sue Bridehead.

items.title: Quiz Q#1500 · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: In which bleak 1895 novel by Thomas Hardy does the despairing child Little Father Time hang his younger siblings and himself, leaving the chilling suicide note: "Done because we are too menny"?
items.explanation: This horrific tragedy in Chapter 40 of Jude the Obscure (1895) shatters Jude and Sue's lives, embodying what Hardy described as the modern 'coming universal wish not to live'.
